title: Indigenous leader Raoni receives palliative care in Brazil after cancer diagnosis
content:
SAO PAULO (AP) — Renowned Indigenous Chief Raoni Metuktire is receiving palliative care at home in the Brazilian heartland after being diagnosed with cancer at age 94, his institute said Monday.
The Raoni Institute said the cancer diagnosis in the chief’s digestive system was confirmed after he was hospitalized in Sao Paulo in June due to a severe intestinal obstruction. He underwent surgery then and returned to the region of the city of Peixoto de Azevedo, in Brazil’s Mato Grosso state.
“At this moment, our priority is ensuring that Chief Raoni is well cared for, comfortable, and close to his family and his people. We wish to share this information transparently, but we also ask for respect regarding his privacy, his need for rest, and his family’s decisions,” the institute said in a statement.
Raoni, one of the most renowned advocates for the protection of the Amazon rainforest and for Indigenous rights, traveled the world for decades to raise awareness about environmental preservation.
Doctors opted for palliative care given Raoni’s advanced age, overall clinical condition, and the high risks associated with aggressive oncological treatments, the institute said.
“Palliative care does not mean an absence of treatment. The goal is to control pain and other symptoms, prevent complications, and ensure nutrition, hydration, medical supervision, nursing care, physical therapy, and the best possible quality of life,” it added.
Raoni is currently resting at home, surrounded by his family, community, and specialized health teams. The care plan also incorporates intercultural and spiritual support, the institute added, which honors his Indigenous heritage and allows traditional healers alongside medical professionals.
By Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press
Banner image: Kayapo leader Raoni Metuktire looks on in Brasilia, Brazil, April 9, 2026. Image courtesy of Eraldo Peres, Associated Press.

title: 8 mn adolescent girls given hpv vaccine in past six months: Govt
content:
HPV vaccine administered to 8 million adolescent girls in past 6 months: Govt
India has vaccinated 8 million adolescent girls in the past six months against the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) under the National HPV Vaccination Campaign.
India has vaccinated 8 million adolescent girls in the past six months against the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) under the National HPV Vaccination Campaign, aimed at preventing cervical cancer, Union ministry of health and family welfare announced on Friday.
“The milestone marks the expanding reach of HPV vaccination through the public health system and reinforces India’s commitment to strengthening preventive healthcare for adolescent girls,” said health ministry in a statement.
Also Read | Bengal health dept probes five accused of practising medicine with fake degrees
Five states —Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Mizoram— have achieved 100% cover of their respective identified target populations. Whereas, Bihar Andhra Pradesh and Assam have crossed 90% coverage, Karnataka achieved 85%, Chhattisgarh, Sikkim, Kerala, Telangana and Odisha crossed 60% coverage, the ministry said. Among States, Uttar Pradesh has recorded the highest number of vaccinations, with more than 2.2 million adolescent girls vaccinated under the campaign.
“The progress reflects coordinated implementation by States and Union Territories, sustained community mobilisation and active engagement of district-level health teams. States have adopted context-specific approaches to reach eligible adolescent girls through the public health delivery network, including in rural, urban, remote and geographically challenging areas,” read the health ministry statement.
Also Read | Addressing the adolescent health crisis through school-based action
With 123,000 new diagnoses annually, India accounts for approximately one-fifth of all cervical cancer cases globally and one-quarter of all cervical cancer deaths, and it is the second most common cancer among Indian women.
In a study published in The Lancet in June, it was shown that high HPV vaccination coverage was associated with a substantial reduction in cervical cancer deaths.
The vaccination campaign was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on February 28 this year. Under the campaign, 14-year-old girls are provided voluntary and free-of-cost single-dose HPV vaccination, with parental consent, at government health facilities.
As per Registrar General of India (RGI) 2021 estimates, approximately 12 million girls constitute the annual cohort of 14-year-olds who are expected to benefit from the initiative each year.
“The campaign has placed strong emphasis on community engagement and credible information, with parents, healthcare providers, teachers and frontline health workers being actively engaged to address concerns and counter misinformation relating to HPV vaccination.”
Healthcare providers, including paediatricians, gynaecologists and experts from institutions such as AIIMS, along with teachers and frontline health workers including ASHAs and ANMs, have supported awareness and mobilisation efforts across States and districts.
“The campaign has also leveraged India’s digital health infrastructure through the U-WIN platform, enabling programme managers to monitor vaccination coverage at the district level, identify coverage gaps and missed beneficiaries, and support more effective programme planning and resource allocation. The national campaign builds on extensive global experience with HPV vaccination.,” said health ministry.
According to estimates, at least 800 million doses of HPV vaccines have been distributed globally, providing substantial real-world experience on their use and safety.
HPV vaccination, initially adopted predominantly by high-income countries, has progressively expanded into national immunisation programmes across countries at different income levels. At present, 87% of upper-middle-income countries, 78% of lower-middle-income countries and 54% of low-income countries have adopted HPV vaccines in their National Immunization Programmes.
Also Read | HPV vaccines for girls aged over 14, consent to use of personal info mandatory for Delhi Lakshmi Yojana
In a 2024 study, published in The Lancet, it was mentioned that there was emerging evidence suggesting one dose of HPV vaccine was as effective in preventing HPV infection and cervical precancerous lesions as a multidose regimen, and in 2022, The World Health Organisation (WHO) endorsed a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule in females aged 9–20 years.
“The growing adoption of HPV vaccination across diverse income settings reflects its increasing role as an important component of national strategies for cervical cancer prevention. All vaccination sessions under the campaign are conducted under the supervision of trained medical officers at government health facilities,” said the health ministry.
It added that government health facilities were also linked with 24×7 healthcare facilities for appropriate management of rare Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI), to ensure timely assessment, monitoring and management of any vaccination-related adverse event.
“With the campaign progressing towards its final phase, the focus remains on reaching the remaining eligible beneficiaries and ensuring that no eligible girl is left behind. The health ministry continues to work closely with States and Union Territories, healthcare professionals, frontline health workers and communities to strengthen awareness, facilitate access and support effective implementation of the HPV Vaccination Campaign,” read the statement.

title: Table for the world: How family, food, and community offer comfort
content:
There are days when the world arrives before the morning does. Before the tea has boiled. Before Delhi has awakened into the furnace of its late-summer heat. The phone glows. Another war. Another wound. Another child crying beneath a sky darkened by someone else’s ambition. Another country dividing itself into enemies. Another day when we are asked to choose a side before we are allowed to choose humanity. And then I look up.
Outside my apartment in my mother’s compound in Delhi, the sun is savage. The heat has teeth. Humidity clings to the skin. Even the afternoon appears to be sweating. Inside, is my mother. And suddenly the world becomes bearable again. The world can be burning at the edges, and someone can still ask whether you have eaten. Civilisation can appear to be collapsing on your phone, and a mother can still insist that you take another helping.
Love does not always arrive with violins. Sometimes it comes with a glass of water beside your bed.A familiar hand on your shoulder. A voice asking, “Are you hungry?” I have needed that comfort lately.
We lost my aunt, Sunita Bhua. Barely a few days had passed when Om Phupaji went to hospital. And then we lost him too. They went within days of one another, as though grief, having entered the house, had forgotten the door. They were loved. Deeply. And the ending was not easy.
Yet, strangely, amid all those departures, there were arrivals. My cousin Anjali and her brother Vikram came from America. My sister Seema, my brother Samir, my mother and I gathered for another journey of farewell. More than a year after the sudden death of my mother’s youngest sister, my beloved aunt Aruna — our Boo Maasi — we were taking her ashes to the Ganga. There is something about ashes that humbles you. All the ambition, arguments, compliments and catastrophes of a lifetime eventually become something you can carry in your hands.
And then there was Luca. My magnificent Bernese Mountain Dog, though even now I resist calling him merely that. Luca was not a dog. Dog is a word far too small for the creature who lived beside us. He was a four-legged gentleman. A super creature of empathy and elegance, grace and grandeur. Majestic without arrogance. Royal without pretension. Handsome enough to stop traffic and gentle enough to break your heart. A beautiful show dog, yes, but his greatest education came from somewhere deeper. Luca had been taught, I often thought, by his own soul. He understood sadness without being told its name. He recognised silence. He knew when simply to be near. Luca has been gone for several years now. But when we travelled to the Ganga to return Boo Maasi to the river, Luca came too. His ashes travelled with hers. And that felt profoundly right.
Those we truly love do not occupy separate compartments in the heart. Family is not a census. And so, my magnificent four-legged gentleman escorted Boo Maasi to the Ganga.
Some creatures leave pawprints. Luca left architecture. He changed the shape of our home, the rhythm of our days, the geography of our hearts. And as ashes rose and scattered, I thought, perhaps, this is what love teaches us. In the end, we do not remember who belonged to which category. We remember who belonged to us. And amid mourning, something miraculous happened. We found one another.
We sat together after too long. We talked, laughed and remembered. Relatives who had spent years living continents apart discovered that we still had so much in common. We had travelled across oceans and carried ashes to a river, and somewhere along the way, rediscovered communion. Grief occasionally performs that miracle when it is not busy breaking us. It reminds us that we belong to one another. Not perfectly. But profoundly. Perhaps, that is why something I saw from my car the other afternoon moved me so deeply.
A young person was walking barefboot. Around them was a little flock of children, gaggling and giggling through the Delhi afternoon. From their clothes, you could tell they came from different homes, different worlds, perhaps different faiths. And yet there they were. Together. Walking towards the Crafts Museum. I watched them disappear into the heat, this small, noisy parliament of childhood, and thought: Oh God. That will make something delicious. Delicious in the way life becomes when difference is not treated as danger. When coriander does not demand that cumin become coriander. When cardamom is not offended by clove. A good meal does not demand sameness. It asks for balance. That is what I wish the world remembered.
My own life has rarely followed the straight lines others drew for it. I was the boy who carried Delhi inside him while imagining America beyond the horizon. The son who eventually had to tell his mother he liked boys. The Indian who learned that identity is not a locked room. It is a house with many doors. My mother’s kitchen. Ghalib and Kabir. Delhi dust and Bombay rain. Urdu poetry and English sentences. The men I have loved. Families I was born into and families I chose. None cancels the other. They make me. Perhaps, that is what I saw in those children. Not a lesson. A possibility. The world, for all its ugliness, is still capable of gathering unlike people and allowing them to walk in the same direction. Some days, the opposite of war is not peace. Peace is too grand a word. Some days, the opposite of war is smaller. It is cousins flying across oceans. Siblings sitting together. A mother making room for her child. A barefoot young person gathering children. It is setting the table. Every time we cook, we make an argument against despair. We soak lentils because we believe there will be a tomorrow. We set another plate because we imagine someone might come.
Cooking is hope with onions. And so, sitting in Delhi, grieving those who have left us and grateful for those who have gathered, I keep thinking about that barefoot young person and their noisy little procession. The world is wounded. The world is weary. The world is loud with people who would rather build walls than tables. But somewhere, even now, someone is cooking. Someone is coming home. Someone is carrying ashes to a river. Someone is arriving from across an ocean. Someone is barefoot, leading children towards a museum. And someone, somewhere, is setting one more plate. I think that means we must not give up. Not yet. Not on the world. Not on one another. The table is still there. There is still room. Come. Sit. Eat. Tell me your story. And if you are different from me, stay a little longer. Together, perhaps, we might still make something delicious.

title: Togo's sacred Voodoo stone augers year of peace and prosperity
content:
Togo
A canoe glided slowly across the waters of Lake Togo, carrying the mystical Aklima tam-tam drum to a sacred wood to herald a momentous event: the 363rd unveiling of the sacred stone.
For the Guin people, the annual Epe-Ekpe or Ekpessosso festival in September marks the start of the new ancestral year.
The traditional "taking of the sacred stone" ceremony is an integral rite dating back to 1663 and started by settlers from the former Gold Coast -- modern-day Ghana.
Believers eagerly await the emergence of the stone, whose colour, which varies from year to year, is interpreted as a sign of what the coming 12 months will bring.
"The stone can be several colours: white, a symbol of peace and prosperity; sky blue, a sign of abundant food crops; or red, heralding a year of famine, war and misfortune," said Wlomo Nomo Combietey VIII Nii Labite, guardian of the sacred wood.
But "it can also be multicoloured, a sign of disease or a major epidemic", added the ceremonial guardian.
This year's stone augurs well for the 12 months ahead, being white.
As every year for the past three-and-a-half centuries, several hundred people, the majority Voodoo priests and priestesses, gathered in Glidji-Kpodji Square, near the southern city of Aneho, to witness the emergence of the stone, known as "Ekpessosso."
In Togo, a country of seven million people, 51 percent of the population practises Voodoo, which has multiple forms.
That is more than those who follow Christianity and Islam combined in the small west African nation.
Dressed in white loincloths and adorned with several strings of pearls, followers sing and dance for hours on end, some entering a trance-like state.
Thursday saw a frenzied crowd gather to witness a select group of believers emerge from the wood carrying the oval-shaped stone.
A Voodoo priest then cradled the stone as the crowd chanted "Helu-lo, helu-lo," meaning woe to evil spirits in the Mina language.
"The white stone heralds a year of purity, peace and prosperity," the priest proclaimed from a small podium.
"The gods have answered our prayers," exulted a relieved Pierrette Ahouefa, a priestess clad in multicoloured beads.
"The rituals began in early June in all the convents and the sacred forest. Each step is followed to the letter," said fellow priestess Jeanne Sika.
The nature-based Voodoo belief system emerged in the late 16th century in the town of Tado on the Mono river, which separates Togo from eastern neighbour Benin.
Followers worship a single god, the Mahu or Segbo-Lissa, through more than 200 deities.

title: Recicla gran parte de su ropa y le pone detalles indígenas, dice la Presidenta
content:
Orgullosa de sus raíces, no recurre a grandes diseñadores ni gasta tanto, aclara
Viernes 18 de septiembre de 2026, p. 5
La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo reveló que gran parte de la ropa que habitualmente usa la “recicla”, además de que sobre las prendas, expertos en costura colocan piezas artesanales, como bordados o huipiles.
Al aludir ayer al vestido que usó en la ceremonia del Grito de Independencia, el día 15, que fue bordado por artesanas muxes del Istmo de Tehuantepec, la mandataria aclaró que no hace grandes gastos en su indumentaria.
Señaló que no opta por ropa de diseñadores internacionales, sino que prefiere piezas más tradicionales y de origen artesanal.
“Tampoco es que estemos gastando quién sabe cuánto para tener una ropa distinta cada vez.”
Apuntó que hay interrogantes sobre la cantidad de vestimenta que tendría, ante lo que aclaró que con apoyo de una costurera que colabora con ella, se hacen ajustes a las mismas piezas.
“¿De dónde saco yo este bordado? La gran mayoría son regalos que me hace la gente cuando voy a distintos lugares. Me regalan un rebozo, un huipil, algún textil. Entonces, tomamos una partecita y lo reciclamos en los trajes.
“¿Por qué uso esta ropa? ¿Por qué me importa? Porque no hay nada más hermoso que esto, que son artesanas y artesanos mexicanos, y que viene de hace mucho. Ahora, los bordados tehuanos de Oaxaca, pues es una identidad. Oaxaca tiene una diversidad enorme de textiles y cada uno representa algo distinto.
“¿Por qué no usar una alta costura de un francés o de algún otro país y por qué usar lo nuestro? Pues porque es nuestra identidad y hay que tener orgullo por ello.”
A pregunta en la mañanera de por qué no mencionó a Ignacio Allende en sus arengas del Grito, la mandataria aclaró que no fue un olvido, sino que deseaba dar relevancia a figuras que no son tan recordadas, como Guadalupe Victoria, quien junto con Vicente Guerrero mantuvo “la llama de la Independencia tras el fusilamiento de Morelos”.

title: First Permit to Clean Up Old Mine Waste Issued for WA State Under 2024 ‘Good Samaritan Act’
content:
The US Environmental Protection Agency has approved the first permit under the its new “Good Samaritan” law to remediate abandoned mine workings.
The permit has been issued to Trout Unlimited, a fishing and sportsmen focused nonprofit that engages in riverine conservation all over the West.
The Good Samaritan act passed in 2024 with broad bipartisan support after 20 years of campaigning by groups including Trout Unlimited.
The legislation was championed by US Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Jim Risch (R-ID) and US House Reps Celeste Maloy (R-UT), Mary Peltola (D-AK), and Susie Lee (D-NV).
It facilitates state agencies and other third parties to clean up abandoned mines more quickly and effectively, tens of thousands of which are known to pollute rivers and streams across the country.
As historic sites often a century old or more whose owners are long gone or deceased, it’s rare that any party can be held responsible for cleaning them up. At the same time, federal laws treat organizations that volunteer to clean up these mines, including state agencies and private groups like Trout Unlimited, as if they are the very polluters who left behind the mine waste.
This complicates permitting and long-term legal and financial liability for any mine pollution remaining after cleanup, disincentivizing the same. The Good Samaritan law created a pilot program to provide limited liability protections for up to 15 low-risk projects conducted by state agencies or other third parties.
“Hardrock abandoned mines are a scourge on the landscape. No one is required to clean them up, so every day they release their toxic brew of zinc, cadmium, lead, and arsenic into our drinking water and trout streams,” said Chris Wood, president and CEO of Trout Unlimited in a statement.
The permit thusly issued to Trout Unlimited will address ongoing contamination of Toroda Creek in Okanogan County, Washington state, about 140 miles northwest of Spokane.
At the site, known as the Bodie Mine, historic mine tailings will be removed and streambanks restored to reduce contamination of the stream by arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and other toxins. The project will improve the health of the broader watershed, part of the Columbia River Basin.
“Bully for the EPA [for] authorizing the first abandoned mine cleanup under the Good Samaritan Remediation of Abandoned Hardrock Mines Act of 2024,” Wood added. “May their efforts lead many more states and communities, non-profits, and yes, even mining companies, to lend a hand and make our waters more fishable and swimmable.”
MORE GOOD NEWS FOR RIVERS: Toronto River Once So Polluted it Caught on Fire Now Is Flush with Fish
While many Americans have never picked up any mining jargon, it’s likely they’ve seen mine tailings before. If you’ve driven by a mining site and seen the long metal chute depositing gravel and dirt into a large conical pile—those are tailings, and they are either stored in landfill type installations or as a slurry in a pond or dam.
Back in the day, however, they were often just stored on site wherever there was space. Many ore bodies that contain useful and valuable metals like zinc, gold, or silver, may also contain—as Wood mentioned—arsenic, lead, and other toxic heavy metals. The process of grinding and separation that allows for the extraction of the former also liberates the latter. Left in piles of derelict tailings, they present a much greater risk of toxicity than when they were underground.

GNN recently reported on Trout Unlimited’s activities contributing to the truly hair-raising numbers of central California coho salmon running up rivers along the Mendocino coast. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration had been contracting Trout Unlimited to remove barriers in the Navarro, Big, Garcia, and Noyo River watersheds for years leading up to the salmons’ return.

title: Más allá de las aulas, los abuelos y sabios enseñan a los niños en la Amazonía
content:
Fecha de publicación:
Fecha de modificación:
Con el inicio del año lectivo Sierra-Amazonía 2026-2027, los escolares de las nacionalidades Waorani, Siekopaai y A’i Cofán regresaron a las aulas bajo un modelo único: los tejidos curriculares y proyectos educativos comunitarios. A través de ellos, los niños aprenden directamente de sus abuelos, abuelas, sabios y sabias, recorriendo la selva y rescatando los conocimientos que sostienen su identidad cultural. Los docentes son los guías y ejecutores de este modelo educativo.
El 10 de septiembre de 2026 se convirtió en un hito para los Waorani, Siekopaai y A’i Cofán. Ese día, las tres naciones de la Amazonía registraron sus proyectos educativos comunitarios y sus tejidos curriculares en la Secretaría de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe y Etnoeducación (Seibe) para preparar académicamente a los niños.
Este registro permite oficialmente a las tres nacionalidades implementar sus proyectos sin trabas en sus territorios a partir de septiembre, es decir, con el nuevo ciclo escolar que ya empezó en Ecuador.
Patricia Peñaherrera, líder de Educación Propia de Amazon Frontlines, explica que cada proyecto educativo necesita el registro oficial del Ministerio de Educación y de la Seibe. Sin ese reconocimiento, los niños de estas comunidades de la Amazonía no acceden a los derechos ni a los beneficios que corresponden a cualquier estudiante de Ecuador.
El proceso arrancó en 2019 con los Waorani, cuenta Peñaherra. La primera fase consistió en un diagnóstico: conversaciones con padres, madres, abuelos, jóvenes, docentes y funcionarios. El resultado fue un informe que se llamó ‘Los 100 problemas de la educación Waorani’. En resumen se detectó el poco funcionamiento de la educación y poco cumplimiento de los modelos rígidos, ninguna infraestructura ni validación de los conocimientos de niños y niñas, docentes sin capacitación, pérdida del idioma, pérdida de prácticas culturales y quiebre del vínculo espiritual con su territorio.
Tras el diagnóstico llegó una pregunta crucial: ¿qué proponen, qué quieren salvar? El pronunciamiento mayoritario de la nacionalidad Waorani fue: “queremos seguir siendo Waoranis, queremos pervivir, trascender. No queremos que nuestra nacionalidad se termine con la cuarta o quinta generación de Waoranis. Queremos que nuestros jóvenes sigan siendo wao, sigan hablando el wao terero, practicando la danza wao, tejiendo la chambira y practicando la siembra de sus alimentos y pescando en sus ríos y cazando sus animales”.
Pero también que los jóvenes adquieran conocimientos del mundo occidental: que sepan matemáticas, lectura, escritura, ciencias especiales, tecnología. “Queremos que se gradúen de bachilleres y también queremos que quiera estudiar en las universidades”.
Así marcaron su ruta y se elaboró la propuesta educativa durante dos largos años, dice Peñaherrera. En la tercera etapa decidieron entre que la propuesta fuera autónoma completamente y separada del sistema educativo nacional o mantenerse dentro del sistema de educación intercultural bilingüe. Ellos optaron por la segunda.
De ahí salió el tejido curricular: un documento que cruza los saberes propios con las materias oficiales bajo temas centrales, como “mi territorio” en el caso waorani. El proceso waorani tomó seis años, por la extensión de su territorio en Pastaza, Napo y Orellana.
Actualmente existen 64 centros educativos waorani, siete siekopaai y ocho A’i Cofán. El promedio de estudiantes es de 20 a 25 niños por centro en estas tres nacionalidades de la Amazonía. Asisten escolares de 3, 4 años, 14, 15 y hasta 16 años.
Solo hay tres escuelas pluridocentes, una por cada nación; las demás son unidocentes. De profesores, solo una parte pequeña es de nacionalidades, ya que el resto es kichwa, de otra nacionalidad y mestizos.
En este sistema de enseñanza tiene un elemento muy importante: La autoridad educativa pasó del Ministerio a la comunidad, a través de comisiones o consejos de educación propia. Ellas definen el monitoreo, la evaluación del aprendizaje y la participación de las familias. Cada comunidad tiene su comisión, pero en el caso de los Siekopaai, solo se conformó una comisión de 42 miembros.
Opi Nenquimo lleva siete años al frente de un proyecto que junta dos mundos en la selva de Pastaza. El presidente de la Organización Waorani de Pastaza cuenta que su pueblo construyó, junto a padres de familia y sabios de la comunidad, un tejido curricular que traslada el conocimiento ancestral al papel, sin dejar atrás la ciencia occidental.
Los abuelos funcionan como una biblioteca viva: la enseñanza tradicional se transmite de forma práctica, día a día. El proyecto no busca un regreso al pasado, sino una educación con dos mundos: waorani y occidental, destaca Nenquimo. “Los abuelos son una biblioteca ancestral”.
Hoy ese conocimiento convive con la escritura y el sistema educativo oficial. Su aplicación corre por cuenta del propio gobierno territorial. La organización provincial se unió con Nacionalidad Waorani del Ecuador (NAWE), el órgano de gobierno máximo, para capacitar a los profesores y así replicar en las escuelas.
En el territorio waorani de Pastaza, seis escuelas piloto arrancaron el proceso hace seis años, con cerca de 60 niños. Ahora la cobertura crecerá a 17 centros educativos, con 160 estudiantes en esa jurisdicción. A fines de septiembre comenzará el primer taller de capacitación en tejido curricular para los docentes de estos centros, antes de extender el modelo a las zonas de Napo y Orellana, los otros territorios de los wao.
Nenquimo explica que entre seis y 10 abuelos y abuelas sostienen la enseñanza en las escuelas pilotos de Pastaza. Uno explica cómo tallar una bodoquera o una lanza; otro transmite los cantos en wao o los rituales que acompañan un embarazo o un nacimiento. Cada niño aprende, además, a leer y escribir. “Si no hacemos esa transmisión, el conocimiento se muere”, advierte Nenquimo.
Las comunidades carecen de agua potable y servicios higiénicos para sus niños. El gobierno waorani construyó cuatro infraestructuras educativas y levanta una quinta, sin apoyo del Estado. Para Nenquimo, el territorio y la lengua se defienden desde el aula.
Nenquimo plantea que los jóvenes waorani estudien derecho, comunicación y otras carreras afines para volver a sus comunidades y asumir el gobierno territorial. Para él, el territorio amplio garantiza alimento, plantas medicinales y libertad para vivir en la selva.
Wilmer Piaguaje dirige la educación de la Nación Siekopai, un pueblo de apenas 825 habitantes en la provincia de Sucumbíos, entre los cantones Shushufindi y Cuyabeno.
Durante años, sus escuelas enseñaron con material ajeno a su cosmovisión, pensado por los kichwas de la Sierra, manifiesta. “La nacionalidad estaba a punto de perderse”, cuenta. Solo se leía y escribía en paikoca, la lengua propia; los demás saberes quedaban afuera.
Tras el diagnóstico de 2019 hubo un cambio de rumbo en los Siekopaai. De ahí nació el proyecto de educación comunitaria, con un tejido curricular construido desde los nueve mundos de la cosmovisión Siekopaai: el mundo del agua, el de la tierra, el subsuelo, la flora y fauna, los cielos. En el mundo del agua, por ejemplo, los niños no aprenden solo la fórmula del H2O, sino que conocen a la mujer y el hombre del agua, seres espirituales que habitan ese territorio.
Sin embargo, él aclara que no se han salido de la línea del modelo del Sistema de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe y más bien se han insertado estos saberes ancestrales para que los docentes puedan desarrollar sus clases con todos los temas y unidades de enseñanza y aprendizaje.
Tienen siete centros educativos, seis unidocentes y uno pluridocente, con 12 maestros propios de la nacionalidad y 3 externos, encargados de matemática, biología y español. El año pasado tuvieron 184 estudiantes y de este nuevo año escolar aún no hay datos.
Cuarenta y cinco personas, entre jóvenes, sabios y docentes, participaron en su construcción. “Es un trabajo por la pervivencia de la nación”, dice Piaguaje. El objetivo no cambia: que un joven Siekopaai resuelva una raíz cuadrada en cualquier universidad del país y jamás olvide de dónde viene.
La población Siekopaai es la más pequeña de las tres nacionalidades y por eso les dicen que la nacionalidad está en proceso de extinción y por desaparecer, cuenta Piaguaje. Sin embargo, cuenta que tienen familias en Perú, donde hay 1 200 siekopaai. A partir de la guerra de 1941 entre los dos países se dividieron, pero desde que se firmó la paz, en 1998, hubo los primeros acercamientos de familias que no se habían visto por más de 50 años. “Ahora sí tenemos más cerca la comunicación y hemos hecho el esfuerzo de contactarnos”.
Piaguaje se siente orgulloso de haber elaborado esta nueva forma de educar a los niños de la Amazonía. Así que recuerda que Siekopaai significa gente multicolor. Sieko es multicolor o de varios colores y paai es persona o gente, “pero ese pai no es una persona cualquiera, es como decir soy originario, nos da orgullo, más identidad”.
Wider Guaramag es de la comunidad cofán Sinangoe, en Sucumbíos, en el cantón Gonzalo Pizarro. Ahí viven 260 personas de las 3 000 que componen la nacionalidad A’i Cofán en Ecuador. El proyecto de educación propia nació en 2022, después de un diagnóstico que encendió las alarmas: se debilitaban las prácticas propias, el idioma y la conexión espiritual con la medicina tradicional.
“Nuestros antepasados enseñaban desde la práctica, desde la oralidad, desde el territorio”, cuenta Guaramag. La comunidad hizo 10 encuentros de revitalización con los abuelos: elaboración de canastos, de shigras y otras actividades ancestrales. De esa manera identificaron la metodología de enseñanza y de ahí salió el tejido curricular propio, con adaptaciones al modelo andino que llegaba desde la Sierra.
El objetivo es garantizar la transmisión de los conocimientos de su nacionalidad y que les permita pervivir en el tiempo como son y cómo heredaron de sus abuelos, enfatiza Guaramag.
Este modelo se aplica desde la práctica, la oralidad, caminando el territorio, recolectando en el territorio, tomando la medicina, por ejemplo. “Fuimos identificando todos estos puntos importantes para crear un proceso de educación propia”.
En clases, cuando toca hacer una olla de barro, el maestro no muestra el producto terminado. Los 49 estudiantes de la escuela, junto a los docentes y las abuelas sabias, caminan hasta el lugar donde se recolecta la arcilla. Aprenden los tipos de barro, cargan el material, regresan y lo mezclan con arena. Ahí entran las ciencias naturales, la geografía y hasta la matemática: cuando tejen la shigra, cuentan las fibras que extraen de la planta.
Para las artesanías, van a buscar el material y recolectar las semillas. “Nuestros abuelos nos guían a dónde están los árboles, las semillas, se recolecta, se regresa, se hace el proceso de lavado, secado y al final hacemos la perforación y empiezan los niños a hacer los diseños de artesanía”.
Incluso, el recreo se aprovecha para afianzar su identidad con el involucramiento de las familias. Cada día, un padre o una madre llega a la escuela con un refrigerio propio: chucula, una sopa, una comida tradicional. “Esto no lo hacíamos antes”, admite Guaramag.
Las clases se imparten en espacios vivenciales y de convivencia entre los niños y las familias. “Es una pedagogía basada en proyectos reales donde se tiene la mejor experiencia de aprendizaje, que no se olvida”, explica el líder educativo de Sinangoe.
Diez personas adultas de la comunidad sostienen el proceso, junto a una comisión de 15 personas entre docentes, abuelos y dirigentes. Para Guaramag, la amenaza no espera: “la globalización y la tecnología nos debilitan como pueblos indígenas”.
La educación intercultural en Ecuador
Son documentos educativos que cruzan los saberes ancestrales con las materias oficiales del sistema nacional de educación. Waorani, Siekopaai y A’i Cofán construyeron cada tejido bajo temas centrales propios, como “mi territorio” en el caso waorani o los nueve mundos de la cosmovisión Siekopaai. El propósito es que los niños aprendan matemáticas, lectura y ciencias sin perder su idioma ni sus prácticas culturales.
El 10 de septiembre de 2026, ante la Secretaría de Educación Intercultural Bilingüe y Etnoeducación (Seibe). Ese registro permite a las tres nacionalidades implementar sus proyectos sin trabas desde el ciclo escolar Sierra-Amazonía 2026-2027, que ya empezó.
Los waorani cuentan con 64 centros, los siekopaai con siete y los A’i Cofán con ocho. El promedio va de 20 a 25 estudiantes por centro, con escolares de entre 3 y 16 años. Solo hay tres escuelas pluridocentes, una por nacionalidad; el resto son unidocentes.
Comisiones o consejos de educación propia conformados por cada comunidad, no el Ministerio de Educación. Estos organismos supervisan el aprendizaje y la participación de las familias. Los Siekopaai, por ejemplo, conformaron una sola comisión de 42 miembros para toda la nacionalidad.
Falta de infraestructura, docentes sin capacitación, pérdida del idioma y quiebre del vínculo espiritual con el territorio. El diagnóstico se hizo en 2019 a través de conversaciones con padres, abuelos, jóvenes, docentes y funcionarios, y marcó el punto de partida para construir el tejido curricular waorani, un proceso que tomó seis años.

title: Therapeutic Family Camps Bring Healing and Hope to Aboriginal Children in Remote Australia
content:
In one of the most remote corners of Australia, a quiet revolution in child health is unfolding around campfires, swimming holes and shared meals. A new qualitative study published in The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific describes how a week-long therapeutic family camp, co-led by Aboriginal women and non-Indigenous clinicians, is transforming the way children with complex neurodevelopmental needs and early life trauma are supported in the Fitzroy Valley of Western Australia. The research, led by Anita Pickard of the University of Sydney together with colleagues from the Marninwarntikura Women’s Resource Centre and Royal Far West, offers one of the first detailed accounts of how culturally governed, recreation-based camps can deliver measurable benefits for families who have long struggled to access mainstream services.
The Fitzroy Valley is home to roughly 3,500 people spread across 32 communities, about 400 kilometres from the nearest regional centre of Broome. Around 80 per cent of residents identify as Aboriginal and belong to five predominant language groups: Bunuba, Gooniyandi, Walmajarri, Wangkatjungka and Nyikina. The region has earned international recognition for its community-led response to foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, spearheaded by senior women whose authority flows from kinship and Country. Yet families there have consistently reported limited access to health and disability services, and children with developmental delays or social-emotional difficulties face elevated risks of mental illness and other comorbidities later in life without early support.
That gap prompted the Marninwarntikura Women’s Resource Centre, an Aboriginal community-controlled organisation based in Fitzroy Crossing, to form the Marurra-U partnership with Royal Far West, a New South Wales-based specialist developmental health service. The partnership operates a two-way governance model in which Aboriginal knowledge and clinical expertise meet on equal ground, delivering a wraparound model of care that includes telehealth therapy, capacity building for local teachers, and the family camp that formed the focus of the new study. The camp itself is held at the Broome Camp School, the closest facility to the Fitzroy Valley offering accommodation, meals and activities in a single location, and was run twice, in April 2024 and April 2025.
Each camp brought together occupational therapists, speech pathologists and a social worker alongside Aboriginal family support workers from the Fitzroy Valley. Children aged between one and eighteen years attended with their parents and siblings, participating in music sessions, sports, arts and crafts, low-ropes courses, swimming and raft building. Behind the playful surface lay deliberate therapeutic aims: building vocabulary, speech fluency, oral motor skills, listening and memory, social and expressive language, and emotion regulation through play-based activity. The camp also deliberately incorporated risky play, activities that require children to assess their own capabilities, test limits and manage risk, which developmental research links to confidence and personal growth.
Crucially, parents were not bystanders. While children played, parents attended workshops grounded in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social and emotional wellbeing model, working on personal artwork while learning about child brain development, grief and loss, intergenerational trauma and practical strategies for supporting children with complex needs. Workshop topics were chosen by the Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Marurra-U team based on priorities identified through the centre’s research, advocacy and community work. Local language and knowledge were woven throughout: parents and children taught the group songs in Gooniyandi and Walmajarri, traditional instruments featured in music sessions, and parents showed the team how to make damper. One Aboriginal family support worker observed that the clinicians’ approach made families feel good because there was no judgement and no guilt.
To capture what worked, the research team used an Aboriginal Participatory Action Research approach with a strengths-based lens, treating lived experience as expert knowledge rather than deficit. Researchers lived at the camp for five days, participating in every activity and recording daily debriefs, an approach they describe as ethnographic observation paired with relational engagement, in which knowledge emerges through collaboration rather than detached observation. Their observations were validated by Aboriginal co-researchers during debriefs and on subsequent visits to Fitzroy Crossing. On the last day of each camp, an Aboriginal researcher and MWRC staff member invited parents to yarning sessions, conducted in English with Kimberley Kriol translation where needed. All seven parents at the 2024 camp and at least one parent from six of nine families in 2025 took part, with findings fed back to the community in person for validation.
The results paint a striking picture of change. Parents described their children as more confident, more independent and calmer, with one reporting that her son slept better and his behaviour was much improved, and another saying camp helped her find ways to make him calmer. Shy children made friends, sometimes for the first time, and siblings shared experiences that brought families closer together. One mother recounted that her son made her toast the morning after camp, a small domestic gesture she read as a genuine shift in their relationship. In one family of a child with epilepsy, parents perceived a reduction in night-time seizures during the activity-filled week, though the researchers caution this was not verified by a health professional and the cause remains unclear.
Parents themselves emerged as powerful agents of the camp’s success. They arrived seeking help with behaviour, speech, emotion regulation and social skills, and left with concrete strategies framed within kinship values and collective care rather than deficit models. Many said the knowledge about brain development helped them understand their children and parent more effectively, and some wanted to carry that knowledge back to schools so teachers could better support their children. Respite proved to be a strategic outcome in its own right: held away from the Fitzroy Valley, the camp freed parents from kinship obligations and daily pressures, allowing them to sit, yarn and connect in ways they said were impossible at home. One parent described arriving and feeling her body simply go loose and relaxed. Fathers, whose engagement in parenting programs is uncommon in the region, actively joined workshops and sports, an outcome both staff and parents celebrated, though the team noted the absence of male staff in 2025 and plans to involve more fathers and young men in future.
The study’s fourth theme may be its most consequential finding: two-way teams work. Parents repeatedly emphasised that the combination of an Aboriginal staff member who speaks the local language and understands the community with a non-Indigenous clinician who is professional at what she does made a big difference, because the message came from an Aboriginal woman too. Aboriginal team members connected clinical knowledge about brain development, trauma and communication to families’ histories and experiences, and explained how colonisation and intergenerational trauma continue to shape parenting and family structures in the valley. Trust built through prior contact with Marurra-U services proved decisive; one mother said she does not leave her children with anybody, but the camp team’s kindness made her feel her kids were safe. The 2025 camp even employed Aboriginal parents who had attended the previous year, which the team credited with deepening trust and boosting engagement.
The authors are careful about the limits of their evidence. Yarning sessions included only parents and carers, so children’s voices are absent, participant numbers were small, and no quantitative measures or formal assessments of language or motor skills were used, consistent with the Indigenous research methodology. Longitudinal data and culturally appropriate evaluation tools co-designed with families are needed to capture specific therapeutic outcomes and effects on education. Still, the study concludes that family-centred therapeutic camps, delivered through two-way teams with trauma-informed practice and local Aboriginal women’s leadership, show genuine promise for improving emotion regulation, social skills, confidence and behaviour in children while empowering parents. Set within a broader wraparound model that includes telehealth and service-provider training, the Marurra-U camp suggests a replicable blueprint: when clinical expertise is woven together with cultural authority, community leadership and relationship, healing follows, and the researchers ask what health systems might look like if every program were built this way.

title: The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
content:
The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
While visiting the Lebanese mountain town Dhour El Choueir, I couldn't shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier.
Six years ago, on August 4, 2020, a massive explosion at the Port of Beirut killed more than two hundred people, wounded thousands, and devastated large parts of the capital.
This August, sitting with a friend at a family-run restaurant amid the pine trees of Dhour El Choueir, a mountain town overlooking Beirut, I found myself unable to shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier.
Lebanese painter Moustafa Farroukh’s watercolor “A Group of Pines in Bekfaya” was painted just a few miles from here in 1936. Born and first trained in Beirut under the painter Habib Serour, Farroukh later studied in Rome and Paris before returning to establish his practice in his native city. Through portraits and idealized landscapes, he offered a vivid vision of Lebanon’s people and terrain. Farroukh became a foundational figure in modern Lebanese painting, his art helping shape a visual language for the country while its political and cultural identity was still taking form under the French Mandate.
The painting of the pine grove was seared into my memory when I first saw it in 2003 in a catalog accompanying a Sursock Museum exhibition of Farroukh’s works. (The watercolor was on loan from the private collection of Emile Nasrallah.) Sursock itself later became a victim of the Beirut Port explosion. The blast shattered its stained-glass windows and damaged the historic building as well as dozens of artworks. The museum reopened on May 26, 2023, with five exhibitions, one of them titled Beyond Ruptures.
In August 1937, the Armenian poet Vahan Tekeyan was also here in Dhour El Choueir when he wrote the sonnet “To a Lebanese Pine Tree.”
I reconnected with the sonnet after returning home. I corrected a few errors in my translation, adjusted the wording and rhythms, and tried to bring the English closer to the movement of Tekeyan’s Armenian.
Here is the translation as I read it now, at twice the age I was when I first attempted it, with many more years of witnessing Lebanon from near and far.
To a Lebanese Pine Tree
By Vahan Tekeyan
Dhour El Choueir, Lebanon, August 1937
Your pain unfolds from the past, O soft-shadowed
pine tree… Barely risen from the ground
you have lost your maiden branch, the trace of which
appears on you, dried and jutting, like a severed arm.
Then countless others followed it, one after another…
Until, once they thought your trunk had grown large enough,
they let your upper branches sprout and thicken,
and slowly adorn themselves with translucent tresses.
And upon them too, how many fresh traces of the saw —
all your grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon,
whose open grave you have become beneath the skies…
But you do not at all inspire, O green tree of the mountains,
with memories of so many victims, any thought of mourning;
you ever bring forth new life and sway in joyous mood…
Born in Constantinople in 1878, Tekeyan came of age in an Armenian literary world that would be shattered during his lifetime. Poet, editor, teacher, and public figure, he belonged to a generation whose intellectual and literary lives cannot be separated from the violence that dispersed Ottoman Armenians across new geographies.
By 1937, Lebanon had become one of the epicenters of Armenian revival in the Middle East. Survivors of the Armenian Genocide had reconstituted community life away from their ancestral towns, rebuilding around churches and secular institutions.
Tekeyan participated directly in this process of revival. In September 1937, he became the first editor of a new Armenian newspaper in Beirut, Zartonk (“Awakening,” still published today). Tekeyan included “To a Lebanese Pine Tree,” written the previous month in Dhour El Choueir, in the paper’s inaugural issue, nestled among news items ranging from the upcoming parliamentary elections in French Mandate Lebanon and domestic politics in Palestine to the Spanish Civil War and Mussolini’s visit to Germany.
For all the Armenian resonances of Tekeyan’s wounded tree, the poem is emphatically Lebanese. Reading it in Lebanon in August 2026, I was struck less by what the pine might stand for than by how closely its contradictions seemed to belong to the country around me.
The poem begins with history lodged in the body. “Your pain unfolds from the past,” Tekeyan tells the tree.
The first wound appears low on the trunk. The lost branch resembles a human limb, its trace “dried and jutting, like a severed arm.” Before long, the instrument of amputation appears explicitly: the saw.
The mutilations accumulate. “Then countless others followed it, one after another.” Yet the tree continues upward. Its higher branches are eventually allowed to sprout and thicken, adorning themselves with “translucent tresses.” Tekeyan lets us glimpse flourishing before making us look again: those branches, too, bear “fresh traces of the saw.”
And then Tekeyan shifts the metaphor. The injured body becomes a genealogy. Its branches are its “grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon.” The ancestor remains standing as its descendants disappear around it.
Tekeyan then reverses the natural order of generations: The ancestor becomes the grave of its descendants, “whose open grave you have become beneath the skies.”
Everything in the sonnet seems to carry us toward grief.
Until it doesn’t.
“But you do not at all inspire,” Tekeyan writes, “any thought of mourning.”
And he tells us why: “You ever bring forth new life.”
In writing and conversation about Lebanon, the word “resilience” is tossed around liberally. But endlessly celebrating people’s resilience can normalize what they are repeatedly forced to endure.
No less common in Western media is the portrayal of Lebanon as hedonistic: its nightlife and crowded beach clubs, where the party continues amid economic collapse and political crisis. For decades, such coverage has treated the revival of Beirut’s bars and clubs as evidence that the country is “back.”
It is a seductive shorthand. But like the celebration of resilience, this framing romanticizes precarity and escapism while obscuring the scars of war and the uneven costs of crisis.
Tekeyan’s pine offers us something more compelling. Farroukh’s pines, in turn, offer a key to reading the poem.
Farroukh’s trees stand together.
Seen in this light, what is often flattened into hedonism may instead be understood as one manifestation of solidarity: an insistence on gathering with friends and family against the odds, even while bearing the traces of violence.
My grandparents were child survivors of the Armenian Genocide who found refuge in Lebanon, where my parents and I were born. I grew up during the Lebanese Civil War and came of age in its aftermath. When I first translated Tekeyan’s poem in 2003 and encountered Farroukh’s painting in the exhibition catalog that same year, I was still living there. Three years later came another war. Soon thereafter, I moved to the United States.
But it was only in Dhour El Choueir, in August 2026, that the poem and the painting came together for me, revealing something about Lebanon beyond the familiar scripts.
The wounds remain. The tree sways.

title: Where the past lives in the present – Amerindian heritage comes alive at Sophia
content:
By Mishael Henry
There was something about the scenery at the Sophia Exhibition Site that made time feel almost timeless. Even with the influx of patrons, the colourful displays, and the steady hum of conversation, Guyana’s past seemed to find a place in the present – etched into pieces of wood, woven from straw and Tibisiri, and fashioned into objects carrying stories handed down through generations. This year’s celebrations are being held under the theme, ‘Observing Our Cultural Heritage During Our Diamond Jubilee: Honouring Our Traditions, Culture, and Contributions.’ Quite by coincidence, the Guyana Times encountered artisan Roland Taylor at his booth, immersed in the craft to which he has devoted himself. His work had already begun attracting attention, with several pieces purchased and others bearing the unmistakable signs of a successful exhibition – sold-out pieces. For Taylor, however, the attraction was about more than simply purchasing a beautiful object.
“The vibes are good. You just have to come yourself to get the vibes down here at Sophia,” he said, encouraging members of the public to visit the exhibition. “If you don’t come, you miss out. I understand you have to wait till next year. So, the vibes are right down here. You have to come to Sophia Exhibition Site and get the real thing.” With the exhibition continuing into the following day, Taylor urged people not to miss the opportunity to experience the displays, noting that activities begin at 10:00h. Taylor explained that his creations begin with simple tools and carefully selected pieces of timber. After the initial carving comes the finishing process, requiring several grades of sandpaper. “And I use all the finishing sandpaper, like from starting with the big grains till the finishing grain,” he added. Yet Taylor’s work is not merely about transforming a piece of wood into something pleasing to the eye. Among his creations are representations of the owl, the mystical man, the jaguar, and the black panther – figures rooted in Indigenous beliefs, traditions, and understandings of the natural world. Pointing to the mystical man, Taylor explained that the piece speaks to the different tribes and the distinct forms of power and belief that exist within Indigenous communities. He stressed that no tribe could simply be considered more powerful than another, since each community possesses its own beliefs, traditions, and understanding of power. “You cannot say, ‘Oh, I’m stronger than another tribe.’ That tribe has its own power within their life,” he said. For Taylor, the forest itself is filled with signs and meanings – things that may appear mysterious or frightening to an outsider but carry significance to those who understand the traditional knowledge of Indigenous communities. Among the most intriguing of his pieces is the owl board, which he described as being connected to secret knowledge within Indigenous livelihood. According to Taylor, the owl has traditionally been regarded as a messenger capable of revealing certain occurrences within a family or community. He explained that when a girl becomes pregnant, the owl may come and howl, serving as a signal to those familiar with the traditional understanding of the forest. The bat too has its own place in this traditional system of signs. Taylor explained that when a boy child is expected, the bat is believed to bring a seed and drop it in the yard or along a path where people walk. For those who inherit and understand these traditions, such occurrences are not simply random events. They form part of a wider body of knowledge – signals read from the natural world and understood within the community. When asked about the sizable pieces of wood from which some of his sculptures were fashioned, Taylor explained that he does not necessarily have to travel far to find his raw materials. “One here is from my backyard,” he said, pointing to one piece. Another, he explained, was found along the main road.
A sculpture representing a jaguar, for instance, was priced at $100,000, while another piece was priced at $80,000 and another at $60,000. Some of Taylor’s work had already been sold, demonstrating the value visitors place not only on the craftsmanship but also on the cultural stories embodied in each piece. Among his creations was also a horse’s head incorporating an Indigenous man. Taylor connected the work to the Indigenous communities of the Rupununi savannahs, where horses have long been part of community life. A few booths away, another expression of Indigenous heritage was taking shape – this time not beneath the blade of a chisel, but through the patient weaving of straw and Tibisiri.
Older Guyana
Martina Samuels sat at her booth as visitors moved through the exhibition, surrounded by objects that spoke quietly of an older Guyana. There were headbands associated with Amerindian traditional leadership, including those worn by Toshaos and chiefs, as well as necklaces and other forms of adornment.
Behind her stood earrings fashioned from Tibisiri and feathers, fittingly displayed during a month when Indigenous identity and culture occupy a particularly prominent place in the national consciousness. Tibisiri is a thin, pale, flexible fiber or straw-like material extracted from the young leaves and shoots of the Ité palm (also called the eté or eta palm) by the indigenous Amerindian people of Guyana. The display continued with traditional clothing, including women’s bras and skirts, alongside bags, fruit bowls, jewelry boxes, arambos, fans, and trays. There was also a small matapi and a sifter, traditional implements associated with the preparation of cassava bread. Asked whether it was important for Indigenous people to know and preserve their culture, she was unequivocal. “I think it’s important because we are Arawaks. We deal with tibisiri, straw, and that’s why we try to, you know, hand it down to the younger ones as they come. Because when we get old, we try to hand down to the young ones that they must know the work, what to do,” she said.
Traditional flavours
Meanwhile, the taste of Indigenous culture was also being served up at the exhibition, as Jason and Michelle’s Churrascaria offered visitors an opportunity to experience traditional and regional flavours. “Well, we usually do the kebabs. We have beef, chicken, pork, calabrese. They do the kebab on the stick. You can have a look if you want to ; we also do – you can see – the beef, and then we have the chicken, we have pork, and we have the calabrese. We also have cassava bread. We also do a Brazilian cocktail; it’s called caipirinha,” she added. For Jason and Michelle’s Native Churrascaria, the Heritage Exhibition has also become a place where culture is shared across communities. “This is actually our third year selling with the Heritage Exhibition,” they explained.
While they are not from a particular region, they noted that their mother is from Region Eight. For them, however, the significance of the exhibition stretches far beyond their own Indigenous heritage. “Well, it’s a very wonderful feeling because it’s not just only about our Indigenous people. It’s about all the different races coming together to see our culture, what it’s about. So, it’s a really wonderful feeling,” they said. Amerindian Heritage Month is celebrated annually throughout September, with activities being held across Guyana to promote greater recognition, appreciation and respect for the culture and contributions of the country’s First Peoples.

title: Reducen la pobreza en Sonora mediante programas sociales
content:
Reducen la pobreza en Sonora mediante programas sociales
La estrategia entre la Federación y el estado logró sacar de este rubo a 456 mil personas en 5 años
Con el respaldo del gobierno federal encabezado por la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, la política de desarrollo social instrumentada en el estado de Sonora ha beneficiado a más de un millón de habitantes mediante una inversión anual de 20 mil millones de pesos.
Bajo el compromiso institucional del gobernador Alfonso Durazo de generar oportunidades de desarrollo integral para la población local, un total de 456 mil sonorenses lograron superar la condición de pobreza durante los últimos cinco años.
La estrategia asistencial articula programas prioritarios como las pensiones para adultos mayores y personas con discapacidad, Pensión Mujeres Bienestar, Salud Casa por Casa, Sembrando Vida, Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro y los esquemas de becas Rita Cetina y Benito Juárez.
Apoyo económico para familias vulnerables
De forma complementaria, durante 2026 se canalizaron 200 millones de pesos al Programa de Fortalecimiento Económico para las Familias Vulnerables, presupuesto distribuido entre más de 16 mil hogares de los 72 municipios de la entidad para otorgar un ingreso extraordinario destinado a solventar gastos básicos.
En materia de atención a sectores prioritarios, la Pensión a Personas con Discapacidad destina 96 millones de pesos para beneficiar a 14 mil niñas y niños.
La entidad constituyó el programa Beca Terapia con un fondo de 117 millones de pesos para más de 9 mil 200 personas con trastorno del espectro autista.
Incentivos para la juventud en Sonora
Paralelamente, como incentivo para la juventud, el Ejecutivo estatal incrementó el galardón económico del Premio Estatal de la Juventud a 200 mil pesos para el primer lugar en 2026, ampliando además el margen de cobertura de 10 a 48 ganadores anuales.

title: Colombia’s Indigenous guardians adapt as pressures mount on the ‘Heart of the World’
content:
- Indigenous Wiwa families in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta are moving farther downslope in an effort to preserve community cohesion amid climate and security pressures.
- The mountain range’s Indigenous nations continue to hold to a “law of origin” that guides their path amid intensifying pressures from armed violence, resource extraction, and climate change.
- Wiwa leaders describe sacred sites, rivers and forests as “living curricula,” inseparable from cultural and ecological responsibilities.
- Recent protections have expanded the protected parts of the Sierra Nevada and prohibited new bids for mining and fossil fuel extraction.
RIOHACHA, Colombia — Amid the low slopes of a tropical dry forest, families from the Wiwa community of Gomke are building a new home.
Their ancestral settlement lies higher on a lush mountain in the town of Dibulla, overlooking the Caribbean coast in Colombia’s Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta.
Across this region, many Indigenous communities have been forcibly displaced by climate-related disasters or uprooted by armed actors. Gomke’s move to lower terrain, however, is described by community representatives as voluntary: a collectively led adaptation strategy to protect social, educational and spiritual cohesion amid intensifying climate pressures and the presence of paramilitary groups.
They call their new settlement Shegunamke.
The Wiwa have also acquired other parcels of land elsewhere in the Sierra, including at higher elevations. “We have left [those] untouched so that rivers, springs and bodies of water do not die,” said Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo, rector of Shenzhawimaku, the Wiwa educational institution that combines conventional learning with the community’s language, culture, knowledge systems and relationship to the territory.
“If we begin clearing and cutting into the páramo [ecosystem], how can we guarantee life for those living below?”
Across the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, known to its peoples as Gonawindúa, or the “Heart of the World,” the four Indigenous nations of Arhuaco, Kankuamo, Kogui and Wiwa are navigating deep changes driven by agro-industrial expansion, legal and illegal mining (driven by rising global gold prices), the return of paramilitary violence tied to the drug trade, and accelerating climate impacts within and around the Línea Negra, their ancestral network of sacred sites.
These changes are intensifying pressures on ancestral lands and pushing communities to abandon homes, territories, and cultural practices.
Amid all this, the communities can still fall back on the spiritual and political framework known as “the law of origin,” which defines the interdependence of Mother Earth and all forms of life. It offers a way to deal with these changes, resist the pressures, and hold on to fundamental truths about humanity’s relationship with nature, life, and existence.
Knowledge as inseparable from territory
Within this cosmovision, the Sierra is not property or a collection of exploitable resources; for the communities, it’s a single living organism encompassing forests, rivers, wildlife, sacred sites, and human communities.
The law of origin governs this fragile equilibrium. This ancestral code guides the four Indigenous nations of the Sierra in maintaining environmental and cosmic order. As the mountain’s traditional guardians, the four nations view commercial resource extraction as direct violence against Mother Earth.
Mineral and energy resources — gold, coal, oil, gas, salt — are understood as her vital organs; extracting them is thought to degrade the natural architecture sustaining life. Yet they continue to be extracted: data analyzed by the Interamerican Association for Environmental Defense (AIDA) show that at least 120 active mining titles and more than 90 pending applications overlap the Línea Negra.
For Luis Enrique Salcedo Zalabata, governor of the Arhuaco Cabildo of Magdalena and La Guajira, upholding ancestral responsibilities has grown increasingly difficult. When private developments, mining and armed conflict restrict access to sacred sites, and agro-industrial and climate pressures transform surrounding ecosystems, territorial knowledge risks disappearing with the elders who preserve it.
The human consequences became visible in Serankwa in March 2026, when armed clashes erupted over drug-trafficking routes. An explosive dropped from a drone seriously wounded a young Arhuaco man and injured several relatives, according to the victim’s family.
After the military secured the area, the family was evacuated to Santa Marta and dispersed to different medical centers, an Indigenous health care provider, and temporary shelters. That displacement separated them from their crops, sacred places, community authorities, and a territory understood not as property, but as a living body.
“To be a woman is to represent the territory,” said the family matriarch. “It is to represent Mother Earth. When a woman is harmed, it also means that the territory is being harmed.”
Displacements, such as those experienced by the people of Gomke and Serankwa, requires communities to rebuild daily relationships with new landscapes while maintaining their connections to high-mountain sacred sites where pagamentos rituals — offerings intended to preserve ecological and spiritual balance — are performed.
A spiritual resistance
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta rises from the Caribbean shores to snow-capped alpine summits. Its complex ecosystems of peaks, rivers, forests, sacred sites, animals, and human communities form an interconnected living system. Damage to one part affects the whole, Indigenous authorities say.
Wiwa knowledge keeper Roberto Carlos Coronado Calvo is combining training under traditional elders with studies in traditional education and interculturality. He sees education as central to cultural continuity amid the changes affecting Indigenous lands and societies in the Sierra.
“It allows us to heal the memory,” Coronado said. “It allows us to heal the territory. It allows us to heal the places. And it allows us to heal the languages.”
The Línea Negra’s sacred sites, rivers, forests and winds form what Coronado calls “living curricula.” These places hold knowledge inseparable from the territory and carry practical responsibilities community leaders seek to maintain amid the rapid changes taking place around them.
“At my present level of learning, I hear when the trees or birds speak,” he said. “Birds speak like people. I listen when they tell me what is happening or what is going to happen. That is called listening.”
For Coronado, such listening is not only a spiritual practice but an action guide: it informs land-use decisions such as leaving acquired forest parcels intact to protect rivers and springs.
“Reciprocity. Care for the trees. Care for the waters. Care for Mother Earth,” Coronado said. “We must protect, conserve and nurture that whole system every day.”
Centuries of Indigenous stewardship have produced measurable territorial protections. In 2023, Colombia expanded Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Natural Park by 172,458 hectares (426,153 acres), to a total of 573,313 hectares (1.42 million acres).
Developed with the Consejo Territorial de Cabildos Indígenas de la Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, a collective of Indigenous assemblies, the measure recognizes ancestral governance as an effective conservation mechanism.
The park is home to a recorded 3,057 species of wildlife, including 49 threatened species and 126 plant species found nowhere else on Earth. Notable species include the critically endangered blue-billed curassow (Crax alberti), the Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) and the jaguar (Panthera onca). It also protects the headwaters of about 18 major rivers, supplying water to the departments of Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira.
In 2026, Colombia designated 1.5 million hectares (3.7 million acres) of the Sierra Nevada as the Corazón del Mundo Renewable Natural Resources Reserve. Located within the broader ancestral territory structured by the Línea Negra, the reserve prohibits new applications for mining and fossil fuel extraction.
Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has pledged to expand fossil fuel production and mining and pursue a harder, more militarized strategy against armed groups. While the former plan goes against the worldview of the Sierra’s Indigenous communities, the latter has found some favor with groups struggling from heightened insecurity.
For Coronado, Indigenous ecological knowledge represents generations of systematic observation that must inform wider society. For that reason, he said, protecting the Sierra Nevada can’t be left to its Indigenous guardians alone.
“When we care for the Sierra Nevada, we care for life,” Coronado said. “It belongs to all humanity. Everyone. And we all have a commitment.”

His aunt has brewed the drink for Gawai, the harvest festival celebrated by Dayak communities, an umbrella term for indigenous groups in Sarawak whose longhouses have long been centres of family, rituals and communal life.
