title: Inter Board Coordination Commission relaxes equivalence criteria for foreign-board students with two science subjects
content: ISLAMABAD: The Inter Board Coordination Commission (IBCC) on Saturday decided that Science Group equivalence would be awarded to students of foreign boards who had passed at least two science subjects, providing greater flexibility in academic pathways. Similarly, the forum recommended 12 additional Deeni Madaris for equivalence of their qualifications with SSC and HSSC, bringing the total number of institutions under the equivalence framework to 26. It also agreed to include B-Form/CNIC numbers on SSC and HSSC certificates, making academic records easier to identify, access and verify. Additionally, the commission will offer scholarships and overseas exposure opportunities to board toppers, besides arranging winter and summer camps for high-achieving students to provide them with broader learning, leadership and exposure opportunities. These decisions were made during the 184th IBCC Forum meeting in Murree. “The two-day IBCC Forum concluded in Murree with a series of important decisions aimed at transforming Pakistan’s examination system from rote learning towards conceptual assessment, while improving transparency, uniformity and international recognition of Pakistani qualifications,” a press release said. It added that chairpersons from Boards of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISEs) across the country, technical education boards, and senior representatives of curriculum and textbook boards had come together for the meeting. According to the press release, National Coordinator of the IBCC Forum Inayatullah Waseem emphasised the importance of active participation and collective ownership of examination reforms. He said the IBCC Forum provided an important national platform for boards to learn from one another, share successful practices and develop common solutions to challenges faced by the examination system. The national coordinator also stressed that greater coordination among boards and consistent implementation of agreed reforms were essential for ensuring fairness, quality and public confidence in examinations across the country. “A major focus of the forum was the implementation of the prime minister’s directives for standardisation of the examination system across the country. The forum adopted measures for greater uniformity in assessment and examination practices, which will also support the credibility and international recognition of Pakistani qualifications,” the press release said. It stated that the forum was informed that examination boards in Sindh, the Federal Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (FBISE), the AJK Board, the KIU Board, the Aga Khan Board and the Ziauddin Board had implemented the new grading policy, under which the minimum passing marks had been increased to 40 per cent. Awareness sessions and workshops would also be organised to facilitate implementation of the revised grading formula across the country. Meanwhile, the forum agreed to develop a uniform calendar for theory and practical examinations and formulate common guidelines and procedures for practical examinations to ensure greater consistency, fairness and transparency across examination boards. During the meeting, BISE Kohat, BISE Quetta and FBISE presented their best practices, innovative initiatives and outcomes for possible adoption and replication by other boards. Speaking on examination reforms, IBCC Executive Director Dr Ghulam Ali Mallah appreciated the Punjab government for the merit-based appointment of chairpersons of examination boards. He observed that competent professional leadership was adding value to the IBCC Forum and strengthening the national effort to shift examinations from rote learning towards conceptual assessment. Dr Mallah also appreciated the Sindh government and chairpersons of Sindh examination boards for implementing e-marking across the province, describing it as an important step towards greater transparency, efficiency and credibility in the examination system. He emphasised that the reforms being pursued through the IBCC Forum were part of a broader national effort to develop an examination system that tests understanding rather than memory, rewards genuine learning, embraces technology, and strengthens the national and international credibility of Pakistani qualifications.

title: Culiacán marcha por la paz: ciudadanos exigen un alto a la violencia y buscan a sus desaparecidos
content:
Culiacán marcha por la paz: ciudadanos exigen un alto a la violencia y buscan a sus desaparecidos
Vestidos de blanco, con globos y pancartas, cientos de ciudadanos salieron este domingo a las calles de Culiacán para participar en la “Marcha de la Paz”.
Vestidos de blanco, con globos y pancartas, cientos de ciudadanos salieron este domingo a las calles de Culiacán para participar en la “Marcha de la Paz”, a dos años del inicio de una ola de violencia que ha dejado una estela de homicidios, desapariciones e inseguridad en Sinaloa.
La movilización comenzó en La Lomita, luego de una misa encabezada por el obispo de Culiacán, Jesús José Herrera Quiñónez. Al finalizar la ceremonia, los participantes soltaron decenas de globos blancos y emprendieron su recorrido rumbo a la Catedral de Culiacán.
Durante la marcha, las familias y ciudadanos mostraron pancartas con mensajes como “Sinaloa ponte de pie”, “No más inocentes”, “SOS, salven al campo sinaloense”, “Queremos paz en Sinaloa” y “Prometieron paz, nos entregaron miedo”.
Uno de los momentos más sensibles de la movilización fue la presencia de familiares de personas desaparecidas, quienes llevaron fichas con sus fotografías y datos para exigir a las autoridades que intensifiquen su búsqueda.
Entre los casos recordados se encuentran los de David Antonio Ruelas y José Isaías Ibarra, quienes fueron vistos por última vez en marzo del año pasado cuando se dirigían al Colegio del Aire de Sinaloa.
En su mensaje, el obispo Jesús José Herrera Quiñónez llamó a la ciudadanía a mantener la unidad y buscar la reconciliación para hacer frente a las condiciones de inseguridad que atraviesa el estado.
Mientras el contingente avanzaba hacia el centro de la ciudad, se observó la presencia de elementos de la Guardia Nacional, al tiempo que más ciudadanos se sumaban a la protesta.
La marcha se convirtió así en un llamado colectivo de las familias sinaloenses: paz, seguridad y respuestas para quienes aún esperan el regreso de sus seres queridos.

title: Mali: Mariam Bagayoko continues to impress on stage aged 88
content:
Music
At the age of 88, renowned singer Mariam Bagayoko still has the energy to perform traditional Malian songs with a strong stage presence. She says it's a lifelong passion.
"From the time I was very small, I began singing in the way of my community. Even before I could speak properly, I would join the women’s evening gatherings around the pounding mortars and sing with them," Bagayoko explains.
Bagayoko has spent her life championing traditional music far beyond Mali and fighting to preserve it in the modern world. She's disappointed that the original rhythms are evolving.
"Today, the n'goussoumbala and the yabara [traditonal musical instruments, ed.] are still present in our music. But the rhythms of our homeland are no longer there. The new generation has modernised them and adapted them to the rhythms of other countries. As a result, they are gradually losing their intrinsic value and the original rhythms are falling into oblivion. Worse still, during competitions they now only play the rhythms of neighbouring countries," she says.
Alhtough her father was initially against her musical ambitions, she has been supported by her children, and hopes they will carry on her legacy.
''I leave my legacy to the children. They will know how to sing in my absence. Only last night, my daughter sang and danced in front of the audience just like I do. She climbed onto the balafon to dance, then carried on dancing on solid ground as well; it was unforgettable. If they don’t stray from the path and aren’t ashamed of it, the next generation is assured."
In 2025, she was given a lifetime achievement honour at the Aga Khan Music Awards in London, having been selected from more than 400 candidates globally.

title: Buipe Hausa Festival: National President Tafida calls for vigilance, unity, and youth reform
content:
Audio By Carbonatix
The ancient town of Buipe in the Savannah Region came alive over the weekend as the Hausa community gathered for their annual cultural festival, a vibrant celebration of language, tradition, and economic heritage that drew chiefs, community leaders, and diaspora members from across Ghana and beyond.
But beneath the colorful display of horsemanship, traditional attire, and kalangu drumming, the festival carried a powerful message: the Hausa people are not peripheral to Ghana's story—they are foundational to it.
A Call to Order: Tafida's Charge
Alhaji Ahmed Tijani Abubakari Ali, National President of the Hadinkan Hausa da Hausawa, known widely as Tafida, used the occasion to deliver a frank and wide-ranging address that touched on security, citizenship, and the future of Zongo youth.
His first concern was vigilance. Tafida cautioned Zongo communities across Ghana to be careful about the strangers they welcome—particularly those arriving from neighboring countries without proper vetting.
"We are a people of trade, of faith, of hospitality," he said. "But hospitality without wisdom is a door left open to danger. We must not be naive. Not everyone who speaks our language shares our values. Do your due diligence. Know who you are harboring. The safety of our communities—and of Ghana—depends on it."
It was a delicate balance—honoring the Hausa tradition of hospitality while acknowledging the realities of modern security threats.
The Passport Struggle: "A Right, Not a Favor"
Tafida also took aim at what he described as a "quiet injustice" at home: the struggles Hausa people face in obtaining Ghanaian passports despite generations of citizenship.
"We are Ghanaians. Our fathers were born here. Our children were born here. Why then must we prove what is already written in our blood? A passport is not a favor—it is a right."
His words resonated with many in the crowd—families who have lived in Ghana for generations yet still face bureaucratic hurdles that question their belonging.
Drug Abuse: A Community Emergency
Perhaps the most urgent warning came on the issue of drug abuse among Zongo youth as the Zongo Chief of Buipe, Sarki Abdullahi Mohammed noted.
"Our youth are being consumed," Sarki Abdullahi said. "And we—parents, chiefs, elders—are we not the ones who looked away? The time for silence is over. The time for action is now."
He called on parents to reclaim their role as first teachers, on chiefs to enforce accountability, and on the community to build alternatives—skills training, education, and economic opportunities that can pull young people away from addiction.
The Zongo Chief of Buipe, Mei Martaba Abdullahi, raised these concerns, urging parents to step up and change the narrative.
The Economic Case: Hausa as Infrastructure
Earlier, General Secretary Suhail Abdul Mumin delivered a keynote address that reframed the Hausa narrative—from marginalized migrants to economic architects.
He argued that the historic Zongo settlements were, in fact, Ghana's earliest Special Economic Zones. Centuries before formal regional blocs, Hausa trading networks linked the Sahel to the coast—pioneering livestock supply chains, textile trade, and leather craftsmanship that sustained cities like Kumasi, Salaga, Tamale, and Accra.
"To study the economic history of Ghana without centralizing the Hausa commercial framework is to read a book with its foundational chapters torn out," he said.
Suhail also highlighted the strategic value of the Hausa language in contemporary trade. In markets from Techiman to Makola, Hausa serves as the transaction language that bridges ethnic lines—allowing a Ga woman, an Akan man, an Ewe trader, and a Dagomba merchant to bargain, agree, and prosper together.
With over 150 million speakers across West and Central Africa, he argued, Hausa is Ghana's organic diplomatic and commercial bridgehead into the largest markets in Africa—an untapped asset for economic diplomacy under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
A People of Builders
As the festival drew to a close, Tafida reminded his people of their strength.
"We are not beggars at Ghana's table. We are builders. We built the markets. We built the trade routes. We will build the future—but only if we first build ourselves."
It was a message that resonated long after the drums fell silent—a call to order, a call to unity, and a call to pride.
About the Hadinkan Hausa da Hausawa
The Hadinkan Hausa da Hausawa is a worldwide organization dedicated to the promotion of Hausa language, culture, and socio-economic development in Ghana and around the globe.
The annual Hausa Festival serves as a platform for cultural celebration, community dialogue, and economic empowerment.

title: Justice Minister: Jordan advancing comprehensive legislative, judicial modernization
content:
Ammon News - Minister of Justice Bassam Talhouni emphasized that Jordan is advancing a comprehensive pathway to modernize its legislative and judicial infrastructure, encompassing laws, digital services, facilities, and human capital to keep pace with national development goals and rapid technological shifts.
In an interview marking World Law Day, Talhouni stated that law is a dynamic framework that organizes societal life, protects rights and freedoms, and secures the environment necessary for stability and investment. He explained that the essence of legal modernization lies in shifting from a reactive tool for problem-solving after a crisis occurs to a proactive instrument capable of anticipating transformations.
Talhouni stressed that citizens remain the focal point of the legislative and reform process, noting that a law's quality is measured by its capacity to achieve its intended objective and reflect positively on people's lives. The ministry carefully evaluates proposed legislation against specific criteria, including responsiveness, constitutional harmony, and socio-economic impact.
Rapid advancements require rethinking how laws are drafted to anticipate future transformations in business, commerce, and social interactions. Talhouni asserted that forward-looking legislation requires early reading of emerging shifts, stakeholder engagement, and rigorous legislative impact assessments throughout a law's lifecycle.
Turning to digital transformation, Talhouni affirmed that technology has become central to modernizing justice. The ministry is leveraging tech to re-engineer workflows, simplify services, and minimize time and financial costs. Milestones in this digital pivot include expanding e-services, remote court trials, electronic archiving, and digital signatures.
Regarding artificial intelligence, Talhouni noted that emerging technologies present complex questions regarding liability, privacy, data protection, and digital rights, requiring a balance between encouraging innovation and safeguarding the rule of law.
On the economic front, Talhouni stressed that stable, transparent laws and swift dispute resolution mechanisms serve as cornerstone determinants of national competitiveness. He pointed to the development of alternative dispute resolution frameworks, highlighting that the draft Arbitration Law for 2026 and the establishment of the Jordanian International Arbitration Center represent decisive steps toward providing flexible tools to safeguard business and investment.
Addressing access to justice, Talhouni underscored that financial capacity should never act as a barrier to litigation, affirming the importance of legal aid and streamlined digital outreach to bring justice closer to everyday citizens.
Reaffirming the principle of the rule of law, Talhouni concluded that public trust is forged through fair, transparent, and effective application, ensuring that Jordanian law remains clear, fair, and adaptable to future change.

title: Tammy Eagle Bull Is Weaving Indigenous Design Into Modern Architecture
content:
As extreme weather intensifies and America’s housing crisis deepens, it’s becoming clear that the conventional ways in which we build new structures are no longer working. In response, some architects are starting to place greater weight on weaving resiliency, cultural literacy, and a deep understanding of the natural environment into their work.
Tammy Eagle Bull has been advocating for these practices for decades. As the first Indigenous woman licensed to practice architecture in the United States, she has spent her career incorporating the historical and cultural knowledge of Indigenous tribes into her work. For many years that has meant designing for tribal communities, like the Porcupine School on South Dakota's Pine Ridge Reservation, which was the state's first LEED Silver-certified school, or the Oglala Lakota Artspace, which was designed around the Lakota belief that stars are connected to "sacred histories, stories, and knowledge." Still, she knew these approaches weren’t only relevant to tribal projects. "There's an [Indigenous] philosophy and methodology and pedagogy that is very applicable to everything that architects and designers do," Eagle Bull tells TIME.
Where conventional architectural practices are often guided by technical factors like zoning, Eagle Bull takes a different approach. "I like to go further back into the deep temporality of the site,” she says. “What was it originally? Who lived here? How did they live?"
She says this is especially important when thinking about extreme heat in a place like Phoenix, which had a record 113 consecutive days of 100-plus degree temperatures in 2024. "People are like, 'This is so inhospitable. It's too hot. People can't thrive here,'" she says. "[But] people did. They had thriving cities, they had agriculture, and they were able to sustain life. And so, if we look back, we can see that living in modern day Phoenix shouldn't be such a struggle. There were strategies that were employed to manage water and to manage heat."
These design principles are at the root of many modern models, says Eagle Bull, such as the “Passive House” concept, in which the built environment is crafted to work with things like weather systems and wind flows, and “life-centered design,” which takes local ecology and circularity into consideration. "The heart of all that is really what Indigenous design has been practicing for millennia," she says.
As a professor of practice at Arizona State University’s Design School, Eagle Bull is helping educate the next generation of architects in these design principles. For example, some of her students recently imagined solutions for unhoused Indigenous populations in Phoenix, focusing on how shelters might be deployed quickly and safely while still centering Native culture and practices. One idea floated was co-housing, which isn't typically embraced in shelters, where men and women tend to be separated. But Eagle Bull argues these kinds of approaches have their place. "There are a lot of times where it's an extended family, maybe the son's taking care of the mother or the grandmother," she explains. "So the idea is being flexible, employing different strategies and ideas in a balance that can work best for whatever situation."
In 2025, Eagle Bull became the director of a new Master's program at ASU. The M.S. in Indigenous Placekeeping and Design was founded by Wanda Dalla Costa, the first First Nations woman to be a licensed architect in Canada and a leading figure in Indigenous design in North America. It is one of only a handful of degree programs in the U.S. that focuses on both the history and practical application of Indigenous design. "There are a lot of things that we can learn from [Indigenous] cultural practices," Eagle Bull says. "They can help us not only manage the ecology and environment, but also how people exist with each other and thrive and create places that support who they are and support their community."

title: How a Secret Orangutan Breeding Program Is Creating a Baby Boom
content:
“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.
Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.
It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.
Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.
“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.
The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.
“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.
“We’ve had a very good, happy outcome,” she says. It all started in February 2025 when the Indianapolis Zoo welcomed Edi, a healthy baby boy. After that, Weila was delivered at the Hogle Zoo in Utah in June; Bintang arrived at the Los Angeles Zoo, and in December, the Memphis Zoo welcomed Ruhana. Peterson, the associate primates curator at the Memphis Zoo says being present for that moment was a “remarkable experience.” The run of babies has continued this year, with baby girls born at the Cameron Park Zoo in Waco, Texas, Sedgwick County Zoo in Wichita, Kansas, and Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana. Just a few months ago, the Denver Zoo welcomed a baby boy named Rambutan.
Humans share over 90 percent of their DNA with orangutans, a figure well-evidenced in how they breed and give birth. Orangutans in the program are routinely given human birth control and human prenatal vitamins; they’re taught to pee on human pregnancy tests; they gestate for nearly nine months; and after humans, their offspring have the longest childhood of any mammal. While C-sections like Jahe’s are rare, some zoos keep ob-gyns on call for their orangutans and other primates.
“Looking at their eyes and their hands, it’s like a mirror,” says Matthew Lenyo, assistant curator of predators at Denver Zoo. “It’s humbling.”
As with humans, maternal behaviors are learned; training is a critical part of ensuring the health of orangutan babies. For first-time mom Hesty, the Sumatran orangutan at the Denver Zoo, training involved teaching her to pass the baby to and from keepers for essential health checks and nursing since Hesty’s mother had struggled with it.
For many zoos, prebirth training involves other orangutans in their care too. To be successful, this training requires a deep and hard-earned trust between keepers and these animals, and can prove invaluable if an orangutan cannot be cared for by their biological mother.
That happened at the Hogle Zoo, when Weila’s biological mom failed to bond with her. She was hand-reared by keepers while they prepared Acara—a proven foster who raised her younger brother—to take over as mom using a stuffed animal as a proxy. They slowly introduced the two to each other, rewarding Acara for properly handling Weila. “She also has a gentle behavior” and uses a very gentle touch, says Hannah Comstock, the animal care supervisor of primates at Hogle Zoo. The pair live together full-time now. Acara is a model parent, and Weila is thriving; she has even started adopting some of Acara’s mannerisms.
Still, zookeepers aim to be as hands-off as possible. “We do all this work, but then at the same time, the best outcome is when you’re not needed,” says Lenyo.
It’s estimated that there are around 100,000 Bornean orangutans and 11,000 Sumatran orangutans left in the wild. The population of Tapanuli orangutans is even more dire, with estimates indicating a few more than 700 are left in the wild. The rainforest habitat they rely on in their native Borneo and Sumatra is being razed to create palm oil plantations, and the great apes are also targeted by traffickers who kill orangutan mothers, kidnap their babies, and sell them on the black market as pets. Some estimates indicate that orangutans could go extinct in the wild within 50 years; some experts caution it could be even sooner, in the next 10 to 20 years.
While these new orangutan babies will not be released into the wild, they are a critical part of species conservation. Zookeepers call them ambassadors; when visitors can see the apes, abstract ideas like climate change and deforestation become more real.
But the captive population also has a direct impact on the well-being of wild and rehabilitated populations: Research conducted at AZA zoos on everything from disease management to quality of life is then relayed back to teams in Southeast Asia. Felicity Oram is a conservation practitioner and co-director of OrangJUGA, a Borneo-based conservation organization. Her research on orangutan’s teeth has been critical in the care of young orangutans rescued from the pet trade who live in rehabilitation and rescue centers. She quips that “captive orangutans can help their cousins in the wild and in rehabilitation centers just by opening their mouths.”
Before Oram’s research, estimating age was an imperfect science at best. “It’s very difficult with size,” Oram says. “It’s just like with human children—you go, ‘Isn’t that a cute 4-year-old!’ And then they tell you it’s 2.” She partnered with zoos, using data collected from captive orangutans to link tooth stages to behavioral and developmental stages. In turn, this research allowed rescuers to more accurately make critical decisions about nutrition, medical care, and socialization, giving these orangutans the best shot at having a successful life—and maybe one day having offspring of their own.

title: Treasured Museum Pieces: The Handiwork of Syrian-Armenian Coppersmiths
content:
Treasured Museum Pieces: The Handiwork of Syrian-Armenian Coppersmiths
Among the various anvils—part of the collection of tools used by Syrian Armenian coppersmiths currently on display at the Yerevan Museum of Folk Art—one stands out due to its inscription: “Ilimkit for deep vessels; made from Zeytun iron”.
"This anvil is called an Ilimkit; it was forged from iron sourced from the mines near the town of Zeytun in Cilicia. Large anvils like this were used to craft large cauldrons, or ghaza," explains Hrazdan Tokmajyan, the creator of the exhibition titled "Tools and Masters", as he catches my inquisitive glance.
The exhibition also features another remarkable artifact from the historical Armenian homeland: a bellows made in the late 19th century.
Following the deportation of Armenians from the Ottoman Empire, it ended up in Syria before eventually making its way to Armenia.
"It's a bellows crafted by Master Melkon from Ayntab. Every workshop had to have that bellows to heat the metal until it glowed and to work it," says Hrazdan Tokmajyan, a painter, art historian, and ethnographer who holds the collection of tools belonging to Syrian Armenian coppersmith masters.
These tools belonged to the collection of Hovhannes—a resident of Aleppo and the last master craftsman of the renowned Kalemkerian coppersmith family from Ayntab.
Painter Hrazdan Tokmajyan, who had moved from Armenia to Aleppo in 1993 to teach, lived next door to him. "We had planned that he would come to Armenia and open a craft school here so that the trade could continue in the country," the artist recounts. The tools, weighing approximately two tons, were transported to Armenia in 2013.
Hovhannes Kalemkerian passed away in 2015, leaving their shared dream unfulfilled.
"I didn't think we would be able to bring the tools to Armenia because the load was so heavy. That is why Hovhannes and I photographed, measured, and dated everything in his workshop. Later, we managed to transport them; we brought over 200 anvils alone. It is an immense treasure—each anvil has its own name, and they are all cataloged; among them are some on which the master himself inscribed notes by hand," the painter recounts.
Tokmajyan says Master Hovhannes’s collection is remarkable not only because it includes tools passed down through three or four generations of his own family, but also tools belonging to other Aleppo-Armenian craftsmen.
Starting in the 1950s, as elderly masters in Aleppo passed away, their family members either sold their tools or entrusted them to Master Hovhannes.
Tools belonging to other craftsmen in his circle also found their way into his collection. The tools were on display for over two months at the Hovhannes Sharambeyan Museum of Folk Art in Yerevan.
For this exhibition, the organizer chose to showcase the tools used by several generations of Syrian Armenian coppersmiths: 140 anvils of various sizes, 100 assorted hammers, calipers, and both small and large chisels designed for engraving copper objects. Alongside these, ten copper household items—such as braziers, a pitcher, a tray, and others—were displayed.
Tokmajyan says these were included solely to illustrate the context in which the tools are used and to showcase the artisans' exceptional craftsmanship.
His long-standing friendship and shared interests with Hovhannes Kalemkerian inspired Tokmajyan to research the history of this distinguished family of artisans.
The artist has chronicled the approximately two hundred year history of the Kalemkerian family in a substantial volume. Published in 2016 with the support of patrons, the book commemorates the centennial of the Armenian Genocide.
The family patriarch, Hagop—a tailor by trade—migrated from the city of Julfa to Ayntab. Hakob’s son, Melkon Khalfe, was a tinsmith as well as a church cantor, scribe, and a skilled vocalist and sharakan expert (Armenian liturgical hymns). His son Garabed continued and expanded upon his father’s craft, working as both a tinsmith and a coppersmith. Over the course of their lives, they worked in three different cities: Ayntab, Damascus, and Aleppo.
Following the deportation of Armenians from Cilicia in 1915, the family ended up in Damascus through the intervention of Djemal Pasha. The Allied occupation of Ayntab in 1918 gave many Armenians the opportunity to return to the city. The Kalemkerians also returned to Ayntab but left for good shortly thereafter. They settled in Damascus between 1921 and 1924, and in 1924, they moved permanently to Aleppo, where the environment was Armenian. The Kalemkerian workshop operated in Aleppo until 1961.
In the book, the Tokmajyan tells the story of Melkon Usta, the master craftsman of the Kalemkerian family. His son, Avedis, was his equal in craftsmanship. Avedis was particularly skilled at decorating copper objects. Although he was a brilliant coppersmith, he is remembered in history primarily as a renowned national hero. Avedis Kalemkerian was one of the three organizers of the self-defense battles in Ayntab.
Tokmajyan recounts that Hovhannes Kalemkerian—the last master coppersmith of the lineage—was no longer working as a coppersmith during his years in Aleppo; instead, he focused primarily on silversmithing. He was one of the last master craftsmen not only of his family but of the entire city. He held a distinguished reputation in the marketplace, with religious leaders and local notables visiting his workshop to commission bespoke silver items.
The Catholicosate of the Great House of Cilicia commissioned him to create the silver binding for the copy of Grigor Narekatsi’s Book of Lamentations that was presented to the Pope.
In the museum, Tokmajyan has showcased around two hundred such masters, featuring photographs and detailed biographies that document their origins, the markets where they worked, and more. These artisans crafted both household goods and ecclesiastical items, the latter being made of silver.
Over time, some of the master coppersmiths changed their trade, or the craft itself branched out into different specializations. The last coppersmith active in the market during the 1990s whom Tokmajyan encountered was Sarkis Bedigian.
By the 1920s, automobiles were already being imported from Europe and America. When these vehicles broke down, they required repair, leading some of the craftsmen to transition into sheet-metal workers.
One of Aleppo’s most renowned sheet-metal masters was Jivan Yeramian, originally from Kharpet—who trained many apprentices. The artist notes that, following the war in Syria, the sheet-metal workers who repatriated are considered the best in the field; they work with exceptional meticulousness—a trait rooted in the traditions of copper smithing.
Rupen Barsoumian, a prominent Aleppo intellectual and expert on the craft, compiled a list of approximately 900 Armenian coppersmiths who had worked in the region (Aleppo and neighboring countries).
Later, in the 1990s, he collaborated with jeweler Hagop Momjian to collect photographs of the craftsmen living in Syria. Subsequently, he and Master Hovhannes added the coppersmiths' personal seals to the archive. "More than 70 masters used stamps; some even had two seals—one in Armenian and one in Arabic. The masters of the Aslanian coppersmith family alone used 20 seals," recounts Tokmajyan, pointing to photographs of the stamps on a display panel in the exhibition hall.
Starting in the 1970s, cheap, mass-produced factory goods displaced copperware from everyday life. Nevertheless, people continued to commission custom work from the masters.
"Wealthy Arabs were in the habit of owning complete sets—featuring several serving trays, water pitchers, and the like. Armenians, too, possessed many such items; during Aleppo’s prosperous times, they would place orders for silver pieces weighing up to thirty kilograms." "Unfortunately, after the war, when people were leaving the country, they would sell these items for the price of the silver, and they would be melted down," the artist recalls.
Tokmajyan notes that in the 1990s, while he was living in Aleppo, Armenians still used certain copper items in their daily lives. For instance, confectioners in Syria still sell baklava on copper trays—just as their fathers and grandfathers did a century ago. Compatriotic unions would prepare meals in large copper cauldrons during major events. Braziers were no longer used for heating homes but rather as beautiful decorative objects that complemented the interior.
During his years in Aleppo, Tokmajyan and a group of like-minded individuals managed to bring the legacy of prominent Syrian-Armenian craftsmen—specifically their copper works—to Armenia.
On May 28, 2016—the day marking the proclamation of Armenia's independence—these pieces were exhibited at the Sardarapat National Museum of Armenian Ethnography and History of the Liberation Struggle.
"The works of the Kalemkerians, and of Syrian-Armenian craftsmen in general, hold exceptional cultural value and are also highly prized objects. Some of their works are in our possession, while others are held in various private collections in Turkey, Brazil, the United States, and elsewhere. The Kalemkerians were a cultured family who understood the cultural significance of the items they owned. They had preserved the works of Hovhannes, his father, and his uncle, as well as the creations of his grandfather—Melkon Usta—and his great-grandfather," says Tokmajyan
In his assessment, these are all museum-quality pieces suitable for display in museums of folk art.
However, due to limited space, the museum cannot allocate two or three halls for a permanent exhibition of these items.
"There could be a dedicated museum named after that family, where both the tools and the artworks would be displayed. Now that tourism in Armenia is sufficiently developed, I believe there is a need for specialized museums. This exhibition has generated great interest; several programs have been filmed about it, and many tourists have visited. Since the beginning of September, schoolchildren have been visiting in groups," the artist says.
During the twenty-two years he lived in Aleppo, Tokmajyan authored five books dedicated to the lives and work of Syrian Armenian artisans; all of them were published through the patronage of the local Armenian community. As Tokmajyan notes, people were enthusiastic and provided the funding for the publications. His latest book, titled Armenian Coppersmithing: Syrian Armenian Artisans, showcases these coppersmiths and their finest works.
"It is essentially an encyclopedia of the lives of Syrian Armenian coppersmiths. This 450-page illustrated volume features nearly all the artisans active in Syria—from the second half of the 19th century through the 1970s and up to the recent Syrian war. Their biographies offer insight into the contribution Armenians have made to copper smithing in the region," says Tokmajyan.
He and a designer friend have been working on this illustrated book for the past ten years.
“The Kalemkerian, Rupen Barsoumian, and Jivan Yeramian families have provided us with significant support in terms of materials. The latter allowed us to photograph and publish their entire collection and provided a considerable amount of copperware from the collection—items that remain in Aleppo to this day. Recently, I requested photographs of works by certain masters from a man named Mahmud Tamar in Turkey—likely an antique dealer—and he willingly provided them," the artist says.
The illustrated volume is ready for publication, but the necessary funds are lacking.
Lusineh Toroyan, Director of Armenia's Museum of Folk Art, is currently seeking funding for its publication. The artist laments the fact that national culture is so often neglected, with its importance acknowledged only when others appropriate it. A recent example of this was the registration of Ayntab embroidery on UNESCO’s list of Turkey’s intangible cultural heritage.
This may be an opportunity for Armenians to secure international recognition for the Armenian heritage of Ayntab coppersmithing ahead of Turkey's competing claims.

title: Residents say Philippines’ Pax Silica Hub will force them off their ancestral land
content:
CAPAS, Philippines - Children’s laughter and the gentle sound of a flowing river are the daily accompaniment to life in a hamlet of about 200 indigenous Aeta families, but members of the community told Radio Free Asia they are in danger of losing their idyllic way of life because a planned U.S.-led tech hub will force them to relocate.
The majority of the residents of Sapang Kawayan, about 47 miles (75 kilometers) north of Manila, are not formally schooled, but they are educated by the ways of nature. Farming cycles are dictated by the monsoon season, and at all times, they are at the whims of a nearby volcano, Mount Pinatubo.
The Philippine government has approved the construction of the Pax Silica hub on a 4,000-acre (1,619 hectare) area inside New Clark City, on land that was part of the U.S. military reservation that included Clark Air Base until the area was returned to the Philippines government in 1991.
Families in the village have already received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) informing them they must relocate from the village because it is included in the development plan, Casamira Capiz Maniego, a 72-year-old Aeta resident of Sapang Kawayan, told RFA.
“They should just have us killed because we will fight for our land,” Maniego said. “We have lived for generations in the mountains long before the Americans came. What will happen to us if they take our land?”
Economic and strategic boon
Defense analysts view the 14-country Pax Silica initiative as a symbolic return of the Americans to their former base in the Philippines, Washington’s staunchest ally in the region. But more than that, it is viewed as a plan to keep semiconductor and AI facilities under one U.S.-controlled roof as Beijing rolls out its own, similar initiative.
The larger geopolitical context, however, is not lost on observers, with Manila needing the support of Washington as it faces territorial threats from China, America’s chief rival in the region.
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has touted the project as one that would “revitalize” the country’s economy and create “quality jobs” for the people. Marcos and top officials have downplayed concerns over potential impacts to the water table and the environment, and fears that the hub would hand too much control to Washington.
“I cannot see how another country can come into the Philippines and, for example, exploit our minerals without the agreement of our Philippine government,” Marcos said in August at a forum organized by the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines.
The Pax Silica hub will enable the Philippines to process minerals locally instead of exporting ore, Marcos said, adding that once realized, it would be “the Philippines fully exploiting our own treasure, our own national treasure, our own natural resources.”
Many people concerned over the environmental and social impact of the project have organized protests, including one earlier this month, where five paralegals were arrested and nearly 30 others were detained while rallying outside a hotel that had been hosting a business forum about Pax Silica.
Regarding the displacement of the Aetas, the affected area sits roughly within 10 hectares (24 acres) of the 1,600-hectare site, BCDA President and CEO Joshua M. Bingcang told media, including Philippine outlet ABS-CBN, on Monday. He said any relocations would affect an estimated 200 people in 40 households, and they would stay within the same jurisdiction.
“They will not be displaced,” Bingcang said. “They will just be pushed a little bit but they will still be in the same barangay, the same community, the same BCDA land.”
Historical rights?
The Aetas have lived in the rough hinterlands as far back as they can remember, but it was in the 1850s during the Spanish colonial era that authorities formally recognized their presence in decrees, which the Aetas now view as historical proof of their occupation of the land.
Tribal elders believe that even without any piece of paper, the government should recognize their “ancestral domain.”
Spain later ceded the islands to the U.S. and during the time that the Philippines was a U.S. territory, Washington considered the Aetas to be nomadic peoples, displacing many to build Clark Air Base.
The Aetas are gentle hunter-gatherers and crop farmers who generally avoid conflict, Maniego said. They have learned over many years how to co-exist with the “lowlanders,” – what they call Filipinos who live in nearby cities and towns – with some Aeta even working outside of their tiny mountain communities alongside the lowlanders.
Visiting the tribal area is like being transported to an entirely different world, where the trappings of modern-day life are absent. Barefoot children walked on the dirt, while a herd of swamp water buffaloes grazed in the distance. The occasional hum of a motorcycle buzzed nearby as an Aeta caravan carrying wood charcoal slowly negotiated the muddy trail.
Private security guards hired by the BCDA blocked the dirt roads to Maniego’s village, however. RFA managed to reach one remote area by passing through small dirt roads accompanied by three social workers.
Tribal leader Petronila Capiz, 63, argued that their ancestral land was crucial to their story as a people, their heritage and the continued survival of the Aetas. The land, she said, has been passed down from one generation to the next.
People, water, and land
Allowing the government to erect a facility here would be a death knell to their way of life, Capiz said, adding that government surveyors have already been spotted measuring the land and studying the Bangot River, the community’s primary source of water and sustenance.
“It will destroy the environment and our source of water, the Bangot River, where we also fish,” she said. “Water and land, without these we will die. Nature has given us these, and they will just destroy it for the sake of Pax Silica.”
Capiz’ cousin, Nelson de Guzman, 57, was emotional. His weather-beaten face was covered in sweat as he called on fellow Filipinos for support against the multimillion project.
Pax Silica, he said, is like “a gigantic leech that will suck the life out of the soil and mountain.” De Guzman is volunteering to organize tribal communities in other areas to express solidarity with their cause.
“We will resist and fight for our rights,” he stressed. “We are not just fighting for ourselves individually, but for the entire tribe.”
Edited by Eugene Whong. Jojo Riñoza contributed to this report from Capas.

title: Lambayeque teje su historia: cuando el patrimonio cultural se convierte en emprendimiento
content:
La historia y el patrimonio ancestral de Lambayeque encontraron una nueva forma de expresión a través del tejido. La colección “Esencia ancestral: tejiendo nuestra cultura lambayecana”, creada por la artesana Mari Carolina Reaño Sánchez, convirtió emblemáticos personajes de la cultura regional en piezas de amigurumi y obtuvo el primer puesto del XIII Premio Nacional de Diseño de la Artesanía Peruana, en la categoría innovación en la artesanía.


La propuesta de la creadora del emprendimiento Marigumi lleva a personajes como el Señor de Sipán, la Sacerdotisa de Chornancap y el Sacerdote Guerrero desde el ámbito arqueológico y museístico hacia una expresión artesanal contemporánea, con el fin de acercar la historia y la identidad lambayecana a las nuevas generaciones.
La colección se presenta en la exposición temporal “Esencia ancestral: tejiendo nuestra cultura lambayecana”, inaugurada el 31 de agosto en la sede de la Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura (DDC) Lambayeque, en Chiclayo, donde permanecerá hasta el 15 de setiembre.
En la muestra no solo se presentan las piezas ganadoras de Mari Reaño, sino que reúne también obras de destacados artesanos de la región, quienes comparten sus conocimientos, tradiciones y costumbres como una expresión viva del patrimonio cultural lambayecano.
Habla la artesana
En diálogo con la agencia Andina, Mari Reaño explicó que cada pieza es elaborada de manera artesanal con hilo de algodón y puede demandar aproximadamente un día de trabajo. Sin embargo, los diseños con mayor complejidad requieren más tiempo debido a la cantidad de detalles que deben ser reproducidos.
“Uno de los mayores retos fue representar al Señor de Sipán, debido a la complejidad de su vestimenta y a los diversos símbolos que caracterizan al personaje. Cada elemento fue trabajado cuidadosamente mediante la técnica del crochet para mantener los detalles de la representación”, afirmó.
La artesana informó que la historia de Marigumi comenzó hace seis años con la elaboración de muñecos tejidos, pero con el tiempo el emprendimiento tomó una nueva dirección: utilizar la artesanía como una herramienta para preservar la memoria, revalorar las raíces culturales y transmitir la historia de Lambayeque, a través de las manos de sus artesanos.
Nuevas propuestas
“Esencia ancestral” también incorpora nuevas propuestas, como personajes en formato de llavero y piezas acompañadas de bases de madera con grabados láser personalizados. Entre las creaciones destaca una representación del papa León XIV en amigurumi, como parte de las nuevas propuestas desarrolladas por la artesana.
Para Reaño, el reconocimiento nacional demuestra que Lambayeque puede innovar sin dejar de lado sus raíces y que la cultura también puede convertirse en una oportunidad para generar emprendimientos sostenibles y nuevas fuentes de ingreso.
Su propuesta parte de una idea central: el patrimonio no tiene por qué permanecer únicamente detrás de una vitrina. También puede convertirse en una experiencia cercana y tangible que las personas puedan llevar a sus hogares, conocer y valorar.
La exposición incorpora piezas de otros artesanos lambayecanos y destaca, entre ellas, un manto inspirado en la Sacerdotisa de Chornancap, tejido por integrantes del taller Artesanas del Corazón.
La exposición
Puede visitar la muestra hasta el 15 de setiembre, de 08:30 a 17:00 horas , en la sede de la Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura Lambayeque.
Más que una colección de muñecos tejidos, “Esencia ancestral” plantea una nueva manera de contar la historia: transformar los símbolos de una de las culturas más importantes del Antiguo Perú en piezas artesanales capaces de conectar pasado y presente.
“Cuando tejemos nuestra cultura no solamente unimos hilos, unimos pasado, presente y futuro”, resumió Reaño, quien apuesta por que la artesanía lambayecana siga creciendo y demostrar que el patrimonio cultural puede ser innovación, identidad y motor de emprendimiento.

title: Thailand becomes seventh South-East Asian country to end rubella
content:
Thailand becomes seventh South-East Asian country to end rubella
The World Health Organisation (WHO) verified Thailand’s elimination of rubella as a public health problem on September 5, making the country the seventh in the WHO South-East Asia Region to achieve the milestone.
Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge of the WHO South-East Asia Region, endorsed the Regional Verification Commission‘s recommendation.
“Thailand has shown that rubella elimination is achievable when strong political commitment, resilient immunisation services, high-quality surveillance and community trust come together.”
The Regional Verification Commission for Measles and Rubella Elimination reviewed evidence submitted by Thailand’s National Verification Committee during its annual meeting on June 22 and 23. A verification field visit was then conducted in July.
Thailand joins Bhutan, North Korea, the Maldives, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Timor-Leste in achieving rubella elimination in the WHO South-East Asia Region. Bhutan, North Korea, the Maldives and Timor-Leste have eliminated both measles and rubella.
Public Health Minister Pattana Promphat described the result as a national achievement. He said the verification was a proud moment for Thailand and paid tribute to decades of work by health workers, volunteers, partners and communities.
Thailand’s efforts to control rubella date back to 1977, when the country launched its Expanded Programme on Immunisation. A rubella-containing vaccine was added to the national programme in 1986 for six year old girls in primary school. Thailand expanded vaccination coverage to all one year old children in 1993.
Rubella, also known as German measles, is a contagious viral infection that can be prevented through vaccination. Infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage or stillbirth and can lead to congenital rubella syndrome, which is associated with lifelong birth defects.
Despite achieving elimination status, public health officials warned that Thailand remains at risk from imported rubella cases. Maintaining high population immunity is therefore essential to preserve the country’s rubella elimination status.

title: At Dastkari Haat, a decades-old collection tells stories from Kutch through motifs
content:
Stay updated with the latest - Click here to follow us on Instagram
A traditional block-printing technique, said to have been around for more than 4,000 years, used to come up with a collection decades ago is among the biggest draws at ‘Maldhari Block Prints, You Have Not Seen Before’, an exhibition that opened on September 17 at South Delhi’s Dastkari Haat Studio, according to Dr Ismail Mohammad Khatri, 67, the artisan behind the revival of collection.
Every sari, shawl, or dupatta, which is on display, has distinctive motifs with historical significance that tell the stories of pastoral Maldhari communities of Kutch from Gujarat. Dr Khatri points to the stepwell motifs on a blue and black sari. “For the nomadic Maldhari family in Kutch, a stepwell was a reason to halt — the presence of water decided where they camped in the desert,” he explains. The exhibition at Dastkari Haat is on until September 20.
The nearly 45 year-old-collection — where items range from Rs 5,000 to Rs 25,000 — has been revived by Dr Khatri of Dhamadka village with his brothers, Mohd Razzakbhai and Jabbarbhai. The family, boasting of a rich heritage, owns a studio in Kutch’s Ajrakhpur, a village where the family settled after the 2001 Bhuj earthquake and named it after Ajrakh, the iconic block-printing technique.
In the 1980s, when Ajrakh was hardly known beyond Kutch, it was this family whose prints got the craft noticed across India. Shabana Azmi and Smita Patil, among others, embraced the sartorial grace.
Speaking about the cultural history of the technique, Dr Khatri refers to the connection to Dholavira, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Harappan city of the Indus Valley Civilisation. For the Dholavira Festival held in Kutch in 2025, he made an art piece with 69 hand-carved wooden blocks and hand-painted details in natural-dyed Ajrakh. The trefoil-like design on the shawl of Mohenjodaro’s Priest-King has been compared to Ajrakh patterns, an evidence that the craft existed even 4,000 years ago, he says.
The Maldhari block prints were going to be presented at least six years earlier in Delhi, according to the family. The opportunity, however, was lost due to the Covid pandemic, and now they have finally found their way to the Capital.
In the newly-discovered prints, each motif is steeped in a historical past. Ladudo represents the rolled straw bundles strapped to camels when these tribal families moved. Fuldi means hawaman or wind direction, which gives indication of temperature and mosquitoes. Koyaro is a spider; Pinjaro, a birdcage; Surajmukhi, a sunflower.
Pointing to the sarees on display, Dr Khatri says, “That’s the Kukadaankh print, which means the rooster’s eye. It was worn by elderly women of the Muslim Maldhari community.”
Referring to a blue and white sari, he says, “This motif here is called Charkaliya. While people call it a sparrow (chakli), it actually represents a madhumakhi (honeybee), helping farmers through pollination.”
Ajrakh is made with natural dyes. Cotton and silk are among the preferred fabrics for the block printing technique. The traditionally used colours are red and blue. The technique is said to have helped the pastoral community survive extreme weather.
“The natural dyes we use work like wax. In summer, the pores of the fabric open up, so air passes through easily, and the fabric keeps you cool. In winter, the same pores close, and the fabric keeps you warm,” explains Dr Khatri.
Even the use of bright colours holds a meaning. “When someone fell sick or fainted in the desert while working, they could be easily noticed due to the bright clothes in the white desert of Rann,” he explains.
At the same time, certain colours were reserved for certain communities — like green for farmers. That provided “hunting and field logic before modern military camouflage existed,” according to him.
Wearing a black Ajrakh sari with the Kamariya motif printed in white, Jaya Jaitly, curator and founder of Dastkari Haat Samiti, shares how her two-decade-old green cotton sari has turned “into a beautiful blue” because of repeated washing as she points to the technique of mixing of colours for dyeing.
Originally from Pakistan’s Sindh, the Khatri community was said to have been invited to Kutch in 1586 by Raja Bharmal I, who granted them land and tax exemption on their produce. They settled in Dhamadka village by the Saran river — the water was essential for washing printed cloth.
Around 1989, the river significantly dried up and the remaining water was contaminated with iron*, posing a key hurdle. In 2001, the devastating Bhuj earthquake destroyed homes and workshops, making it impossible to continue living and working there. The community then relocated to a new village near Bhuj, which they named Ajrakhpur, literally meaning “the town of Ajrakh”. Dr Khatri gradually secured a Rs 1-crore mega-cluster grant from the state government for effluent treatment plants and land.

title: California flooded Monticello in 1956; Its streets still lie beneath Lake Berryessa
content:
A small California community of ranches, farms, schools and family homes has been covered by water for nearly 70 years. Beneath the waters of Lake Berryessa rests the ghost town of Monticello, preserved in fragments: its roads, foundations and historic bridge still visible beneath the surface while photographs and memories keep its story alive above. The town was flooded as part of a massive water project in California but its legacy has been much harder to wash away. According to The Sacramento Bee, in the 19th century Monticello grew up on Putah Creek in Napa County, and eventually was home to some 300 people. They farmed, raised cattle and created a close-knit rural community in the Berryessa Valley. That life changed in the late 1940s, when the plans moved forward for the Monticello Dam and the reservoir that would be Lake Berryessa. The government bought the land for the project and evicted the residents of Monticello. By 1956, buildings were being destroyed or burned so they would not become hazards when the valley flooded. The dam was finished in February 1957 at a reported cost of $47 million. Soon the valley began to disappear beneath the swelling reservoir, which would provide a major water source for Solano County.
What was lost at Lake Berryessa
Monticello had more than houses. It had businesses, schools, farmland, community facilities and a popular rodeo with the Scribner family.
The valley was also known for its fertile soils that supported cattle, wheat and other agricultural activities. Later, Highway 28, later Highway 128, crossed the southern end of the valley. In 1896 a stone bridge was constructed across Putah Creek joining parts of the community. Much of the land is still under water. During droughts and low lake levels, pieces of the old town have occasionally surfaced, offering a rare glimpse of what was there before the reservoir. The historic bridge has even attracted scuba divers exploring the underwater landscape, states the Sacramento Bee report.
Monticello photographs saved
The photographs came to be known as Death of a Valley. Life never published the full project but excerpts were published in the magazine Aperture in 1960.
One of the most striking accounts of the town’s last days came from the photographers Dorothea Lange and Pirkle Jones. The couple spent a year on assignment from Life magazine photographing Monticello and the nearby Berryessa Valley as the residents prepared to move away. Their photographs documented houses, farms, families and landscapes on the verge of extinction. Lange was a celebrated documentary photographer, known especially for her famous photo of Migrant Mother. Jones had been an apprentice of famous landscape photographer Ansel Adams. The photographs came to be known as Death of a Valley. Life never published the full project but excerpts were published in the magazine Aperture in 1960. Decades later, UC Santa Cruz digitized thousands of images from the collection and put them online, letting a new generation see the community that is now under the lake.
Painful legacy for former residents
The loss was more than just the vanishing of buildings for families connected to Monticello. Former residents were dispersed throughout neighboring communities and some could find no affordable farmland to replace what they lost. Families that had lived in the valley for generations suddenly had to re-create their lives somewhere else. It was one chapter in a much larger story of American displacement. Hundreds of communities across the U.S. have been abandoned or submerged due to dam and reservoir projects. Monticello’s experience is a case study of the human costs of infrastructure decisions that can remake entire landscapes while serving populations orders of magnitude larger.
Remembering a lost community
The Monticello Public Cemetery was moved before the reservoir was filled, and is now located near Spanish Flat. With some 600 graves it has become one of the most tangible reminders of the former community. Descendants still gather there, particularly around Memorial Day, connecting families whose hometown disappeared generations ago. The number of surviving residents has steadily declined, making those reunions more and more important. Today Lake Berryessa means recreation, water supply and California’s vast infrastructure network. But behind the front was another story: a town whose houses had been razed, whose valley was flooded and whose residents had been scattered. Monticello might be invisible on the landscape, but its photographs, cemetery, sunken buildings and remaining family memories make sure the community has not totally gone.
