title: For Years, the Smithsonian Strove to Bring the African American History and Culture Museum to the National Mall. Now, It Celebrates a Decade as a Beacon of Understanding, Community and Resilience
content:
For Years, the Smithsonian Strove to Bring the African American History and Culture Museum to the National Mall. Now, It Celebrates a Decade as a Beacon of Understanding, Community and Resilience
The museum lovingly called the “Blacksonian” chronicles the past and present and envisions the future to tell the stories of Black life in America
On a visit to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, Elizabeth Beckett stands proudly in front of a uniform worn by one of the thousands of Black men who worked aboard segregated trains, in palace cars built by industrialist George Pullman. They were called Pullman porters, and Beckett’s grandfather was among them.
“His name was James Syres. He died when he was 90 or 91,” Beckett recalls.
The first porters were recently emancipated men hired by Pullman starting around 1867 to staff the luxury sleeping cars. They did everything from serving gourmet meals to shining shoes to carrying baggage. Some were even forced to sing and dance.
The porters formed the backbone of the Black middle class, following the path of their wealthier white passengers to save money to send their children and grandchildren to college. That opened the door to opportunities they never had, and many descendants of porters went on to become influential figures in American society, including Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall.
Just around the corner in the “Defending Freedom, Defining Freedom” exhibition is a gorgeous pump organ bought by Pullman porter Henry L. Long in 1911. Museum curator Mary Elliott, whose uncle was a Pullman porter based in Denver, says the organ is a symbol of the importance of the men who formed the first predominantly Black labor union, which was later crucial to the civil rights movement.
“Let’s think about these men as Pullman porters just like we think about people who held prestige in their communities—a teacher, a doctor, a lawyer,” Elliott says.
In their everyday lives, Elliott notes, the job allowed porters like Long “to celebrate their being a community, being Black, being middle-class, even to acknowledge how far they had come, just gathering around an organ and singing.”
Elliott says these are the connections she hopes visitors consider when they peruse the thousands of objects on view at the museum as it celebrates its tenth anniversary.
“I want you to go home and look at something in your own home that has that same impact,” Elliott says. “How does that bring us together in these everyday, mundane moments?”
The museum opened on September 24, 2016, with a staff of about 200 people. It would serve as a living symbol of the importance of the nation’s shared history and the joy of celebrating a journey begun by African American Civil War veterans in 1915 who sought to get a museum built on the National Mall.
The decades-long effort got its final push with the bipartisan efforts of Congressman John Lewis of Georgia, a stalwart of the civil rights movement, and Senator Sam Brownback of Kansas; the bill establishing the museum was signed by President George W. Bush in 2003.
During a recent visit, throngs of visitors wandered transfixed through the galleries at the museum known colloquially to some as the “Blacksonian,” a few crouching down to read the dense signage and panels that crowd the walls and exhibitions. Carolyn Harris came with her husband, Shawn, from Mount Vernon, New York, and says this museum is crucial to teaching young Black people about their history.
“They need to know what we went through to get where we are now,” Harris says. She also thinks the museum is important for those who aren’t African American, to understand “where we came from.”
Quick facts: Celebrating ten years
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III, the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, will commemorate the tenth anniversary on September 25 with a conversation moderated by the journalist Laura Coates.
Founding deputy museum director Kinshasha Holman Conwill feels the occasion is more like the museum’s 20th anniversary because of all the longtime legwork the staff put in. Celebrities—Oprah Winfrey and Michael Jordan, among others—donated millions of dollars to the museum prior to its opening, and $4 million alone came in gifts of less than $1,000 from average Americans.
At the opening dedication, President Barack Obama reminded the crowd how many historians, civil rights leaders, lawmakers and others in the nation came together, across parties and politics, to make this happen. Those gathered at the event were serenaded by the likes of Stevie Wonder and Patti LaBelle.
Conwill says the museum’s founding director, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III, had a wish list of major objects, including a slave ship remnant and a cabin that housed enslaved people. Today, the collection has searing artifacts, such as a prison guard tower from the infamous Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola, which was built on land that formerly held a plantation. Conwill notes that the museum was constructed around that guard tower and a segregation-era railway car, because of their size. Another haunting artifact at the museum is the casket of Emmett Till, the Black 14-year-old who, in 1955, was kidnapped and murdered in Mississippi. The killing of Till became a rallying point for the civil rights movement.
“At the core of some of the questions were: What is appropriate for a Black museum to collect?” Conwill says, referencing Till’s casket and the prison tower. “Should we collect it? And if we do, how do we display it? And that’s why, from the beginning, it has been displayed in a very respectful way.”
A silk lace and linen shawl given to Harriet Tubman by Queen Victoria around 1897 was a gift to the museum from scholar and collector Charles L. Blockson, who also donated Tubman’s hymnal. She was nicknamed “Moses” because she repeatedly returned to the South to rescue enslaved people.
“It’s such an extraordinary thing to know that you are literally touching history, that you are in the presence of an object that was owned by a woman who helped you become free,” Conwill says. “There’s something about Harriet Tubman that is quintessential of the struggle of Black people, and having those objects made all the difference.”
Standing with her daughter between Tubman’s shawl and the slave cabin, visitor Maureen Bobo says she wanted to stop at every exhibit “just to inhale it.”
“I’m trying not to cry, but it is hard not to, because our ancestors endured so much so that we can have what we have,” she says. “Everyone who is American in the world should know this, because they view us in a certain way without knowing, and there’s been a narrative going on in this nation since we set foot in this land about who we are and the way we are that just isn’t true.”
Beyond the high-profile objects, donated images help define the meaning of African American history and culture. Conwill points to the Henry Clay Anderson collection of photographs and the Johnson Publishing photo archives, in which the lives of both well-known and ordinary Black people are captured for posterity.
“Everybody was not Benjamin O. Davis Sr., the first African American general officer in the U.S. armed forces, or Benjamin O. Davis Jr., right? Not everybody was Joe Louis, the great boxer who was also in the service,” Conwill says. Black people “were the heroes and the marquee names, but they were also everyday people.”
Elliott says part of the museum’s mission, and legacy, is giving the American public credit for being able to look at this history in its fullness. “This is a shared history,” Elliott says. “We’re still all in this together. We’re talking to each other, right? … It’s a cacophony of all of these voices. And what does that tell us about the development of this nation in its many aspects?”
Bunch, who recently announced he would retire at the end of the year, put his soul into this museum, and he persuaded others to do the same. He “felt the weight of history” in this endeavor, he says, and realized that he “wanted it to be a museum that both celebrated African American culture and made this the quintessential American story.”
He says he kept “a huge chart” that questioned what each exhibition says about African American culture and American culture in general, and he “sat in every design meeting.” Bunch and the staff fine-tuned every detail. Shortly before the museum opened, those who worked to create it visited and brought their families, to see how their achievement could help transform a nation.
As Bunch says, “I guess the best way I can describe it is a sense that we gave a gift to America.”

title: Comunidades religiosas de matriz africana entregam carta-compromisso a candidatas
content:
A candidata à reeleição para deputada estadual Marina do MST (PT) e Anielle Franco (PT), candidata a deputada federal, assinaram nesta quinta-feira (9) uma carta de compromisso com os povos e comunidades tradicionais de matriz africana. Entre os principais compromissos estão a promoção do respeito a essas comunidades e combate ao racismo religioso.
O ato aconteceu no Quilombo da Gamboa, recentemente contemplado em edital da Minha Casa, Minha Vida Entidades, e reuniu cerca de 100 pessoas. Entre as lideranças religiosas estavam o Pai Anderson de Bamboxê e a Mãe Roberta.
O Rio de Janeiro tem uma das maiores populações de praticantes de religiões de matriz africana do país. Segundo o Censo 2022, 2,59% dos fluminenses com 10 anos ou mais se declaram praticantes de Umbanda ou Candomblé, o segundo maior percentual entre os estados.
Compromisso
Para Marina, o documento representa uma agenda construída coletivamente pelos povos de terreiro e deve orientar a atuação política em defesa de seus direitos.
“Essa carta-compromisso que vocês estão entregando, que vocês elaboraram coletivamente, pode ser considerada como programa dos povos e comunidades tradicionais de matriz africana do Estado do Rio de Janeiro. Esse documento tem que servir para orientar a nossa luta nos territórios, na busca por direitos e na construção de políticas públicas”, afirmou Marina do MST.
:: Quer receber notícias do Brasil de Fato RJ no seu WhatsApp? ::
Já Anielle Franco, ex-ministra da Igualdade Racial, destacou a importância de transformar os compromissos assumidos em ações concretas de enfrentamento ao racismo religioso e de defesa da democracia.
“O que está em disputa aqui não é só a nossa liberdade e o combate à intolerância e ao racismo religioso. É a nossa soberania e democracia”, completou Anielle.

title: Women’s struggles, social movements brought together in new book
content:
Culture & Lifestyle
Women’s struggles, social movements brought together in new book
‘Shared Dreams Woven by Struggle’ documents the journeys of 13 women leaders who fought for rights, dignity and social justice.Post Report
The journeys and struggles of 13 women leaders who have contributed to Nepal’s social movements have been brought together in a new research book, ‘Shared Dreams Woven by Struggle’, launched in Lalitpur on Friday.
The book, published by Voices of Women Media, documents the lives, struggles, and contributions of women who challenged discrimination, organised communities, and fought for rights, dignity, and social justice. Through their personal stories, it traces some of the social movements that have shaped Nepali society while drawing attention to the often-overlooked role of women in those struggles.
For instance, the book includes the story of Uma Devi Badi and her struggle for land, rights, and dignity as part of the Badi community’s rights movement. It also documents the journey of Muskan Khatun, who survived an acid attack and has continued her struggle for justice and dignity.
Some of the stories revisit the Sino Bahishkar Movement, which has gradually faded from public memory. The experiences of Mahari Devi, Bhola Devi and Chandeshwori Sada, who were involved in the movement, offer a glimpse into the courage of women who challenged caste-based discrimination and fought for equality and dignity.
Speaking at the launch, chief guest Sunita Dangol, acting mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, said documenting such histories was itself an important part of the struggle for women’s rights.
“We need to remember that until it is written, it won’t be written. Writing and documenting these experiences is a strong way to establish our own narrative in a society where women’s struggles and voices are questioned time and again,” she said.
Following the launch, a panel discussion titled ‘Women Leaders and Social Movements: Reflections and Practices’ brought together activists, academicians, researchers and representatives from different fields to reflect on women’s leadership and the continuing relevance of social movements.
The discussion was moderated by Hemlata Rai, a Women, Peace and Security expert. Panellists included Muna Shakya, disability rights advocate; Parbati BK, Member of the Federal Parliament of Nepal; Rita Baramu, writer, researcher and digital rights activist; and Jamuna Siwakoti, head of the Central Department of Gender Studies at Tribhuvan University.

title: 264,000 DoorDash drivers are getting money in a massive $131.5 million settlement. Here’s what happened
content: DoorDash has agreed to pay more than $115 million to more than 260,000 delivery workers in New York City who were underpaid as part of a $131.5 million settlement with the city. The worker settlement is being heralded as a historic win by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his administration, who claim that it’s both the largest settlement in the city’s history and the largest involving food-delivery workers in the U.S. That said, the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection began a citywide investigation years before Mamdani took office after receiving complaints from dozens of DoorDash workers—aka “Dashers.” The settlement owed to workers works out to an average payment of about $442, but the amounts due will likely vary widely. Workers who weren’t paid at all or who weren’t paid on time by DoorDash will receive compensation calculated at approximately 200% of the amount they were underpaid. Mamdani said in a statement that the settlement demonstrates how the city ensures workers get what they’re owed, adding that his administration will keep fighting for working people. In a televised address, he went even further, blasting the company’s “greedy algorithm” for failing to count every hour worked. “This was not a rounding error or an accidental mistake,” Mamdani said. “Today, after years of corporate greed and impunity, we are holding DoorDash to account.” DOORDASH: “WE SCREWED UP” DoorDash didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Fast Company, but a spokesperson told The New York Times that while the San Francisco-based company believed its approach to calculating the appropriate pay for its workers was “fair, practical, and legal,” it will use the city’s method going forward. The company spokesperson said the median payment that will be returned to affected workers is about $48. But some workers could be owed checks in excess of $10,000, Samuel Levine, commissioner of New York’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, told the outlet. In a statement to Documented, Samantha Ramirez, a spokesperson for DoorDash, acknowledged that the company made errors and had failed to pay some workers. “Simply put, we screwed up,” she said. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” DELIVERY APPS UNDER SCRUTINY DoorDash is one of several food-delivery companies that’s been targeted by New York over the years regarding the treatment of its workers. In 2023, the city began enforcing a minimum pay rate for delivery workers, which now stands at $22.13 per hour—or the full-time annual equivalent of about $46,000. The city agency that conducted the investigation found DoorDash had violated this minimum pay rate by excluding “several categories of trip time and on-call time when calculating compensable time.” That meant that more than 260,000 workers were underpaid over a period of more than four years, from April 2022 until June 2026. Those workers who were underpaid will begin receiving notifications from settlement administrators about the amount they’re owed, and checks will be sent out beginning in late October. Another round of checks will go out in early 2027, after DoorDash finishes correcting the compensable-time calculation errors that caused the underpayments, according to the city. But the settlement is but a drop in the bucket for DoorDash, which reported more than $13.7 billion in annual revenue in 2025, a nearly 28% increase from the prior year. Shares of the company fell about 0.4% in midafternoon trading on Tuesday, extending a year-to-date sell-off of more than 12%.

title: Un jeune de 17 ans à la tête d’une exposition très atypique à Halanzy
content:
Un jeune de 17 ans à la tête d'une exposition très atypique à Halanzy
Elle retrace l'histoire d'Halanzy et de la Gaume pendant la deuxième guerre mondiale. Un jeune de 17 ans est à la manœuvre.
- Publié le 11-09-2026 à 15h16
C'est une exposition atypique qui est proposée au Cercle Saint-Rémy d'Halanzy. Elle sera inaugurée ce samedi matin à l'issue de la cérémonie au monument aux morts d'Halanzy qui débutera à 10 h 30. Elle se poursuivra ce dimanche et tout le week-end prochain.
L'exposition propose un thème général inédit, celui de la libération de Musson, d'Halanzy et de la Gaume, par la 5ème division blindée américaine au mois de septembre 1944, mais aussi de la suite du parcours de ses soldats qui ont poursuivi leur mission en traversant l'Allemagne jusqu'aux portes de Berlin. Objets de collection, témoignages, films, reportages, armes, véhicules de l'époque… mais aussi l'essayage des uniformes et du barda des soldats pour se rendre compte de l'effort que représentaient leurs déplacements. Plusieurs autres animations sont également prévues.
Gabin Pinsoni, 17 ans, est à la tête de l'exposition
Autre côté atypique de l'événement, il est dirigé par Gabin Pinsoni, un Mussonnais de 17 ans en rhéto à l'école secondaire Ello de Differt, anciennement Institut de Nazareth et Cardijn-Lorraine. "Mon papa est un collectionneur dans l'âme et consacre ses recherches et sa passion à la première guerre mondiale. Son travail m'a toujours intéressé et j'ai décidé de le suivre, mais en me branchant sur la deuxième guerre mondiale. Nous avons consacré tous nos loisirs à chiner dans les brocantes et à visiter les musées, principalement le War Museum de Bastogne. J'y ai fait beaucoup de rencontres, notamment celle de Johan Hissette, qui malgré ses 43 ans, est devenu mon meilleur ami et qui m'a beaucoup aidé dans la préparation de mon exposition."
Le jeune Gabin a limité son exposition à tout ce qui tourne autour de l'histoire locale et des villages gaumais. "Dans mon esprit, il n'a jamais été question de vouloir refaire une énième histoire de deuxième guerre mondiale ou de revenir sur des épisodes qui ont fait l'objet de nombreux films, comme le débarquement en Normandie. Il y a bien les musées de Latour et de Diekirch dans notre région, mais moi ce qui m'intéressait, c'était de transmettre aux habitants d'Halanzy et de Gaume, la mémoire de ce qui s'est passé dans leurs villages et dans leur région à cette époque, mais aussi de rendre hommage à ces soldats anonymes et inconnus venus de la côte ouest des États-Unis, qui ont traversé l'Atlantique pour nous délivrer. J'espère que les gens de nos villages seront nombreux à s'intéresser à ce pan de leur histoire au travers de cette exposition."

title: For Des Marcus, Malaysia Day is about bringing communities together
content:
As the country celebrates Malaysia Day, the 36-year-old Bidayuh from Serian, Sarawak, believes that spirit of looking out for one another is an important part of what brings Malaysians together.
“I know what it feels like to go through difficult times and to have limited resources,” Des told FMT Lifestyle. “So, as I became more stable and capable of giving back, I felt that it was the right time for me to do something meaningful for others and for the community.”
He has put that belief into practice through two very different projects this year.
Born Desmond Anak Markus, Des is a corporate communication manager who also performs as a singer, model and host. Known for songs such as “Cinta Aku”, he was also first runner-up in Mr Native Borneo 2025.
The youngest of four siblings, he grew up in a family where finances were often tight. His mother worked in a factory, while his father was a lorry driver who passed away while Des was studying at university.
Those experiences have stayed with him and continue to shape the way he sees people facing hardship.
His first initiative took place during Chinese New Year this year, when he helped organise an inclusive festive gathering for members of the visually impaired community.
The event was carried out with the support of an events company and the Mr & Miss Native Borneo organisation, with Des serving as organising chairman.
He said spending time with members of the visually impaired community reminded him that people experience life in different ways. It also broadened his understanding of what it means to support others.
“It’s not always about providing something material; sometimes being present, listening, spending time together and making someone feel included can be just as meaningful,” he said.
A few months later, he organised a beach-cleaning programme at Kampung Santubong with Sarawak Skills, focusing on environmental responsibility and encouraging people to care for the places around them.
Working alongside volunteers showed him the value of collective action and how seemingly small individual efforts can add up.
“Individually, picking up one piece of rubbish may seem like a very small action, but when many people do it together, the impact becomes visible,” he said.
Although one project focused on people and the other on the environment, Des sees both as rooted in the same values.
“For me, giving back is about sharing love, care and positive energy. I may have started with small initiatives, but I hope they can grow into something bigger.”
His outlook, he believes, is partly rooted in his Bidayuh upbringing. Growing up, Des was surrounded by values such as togetherness, cooperation and respect – lessons he now tries to carry beyond his own community.
He also hopes Malaysians will become more curious about the Bidayuh and discover the richness of their culture, language and traditions.
Music, he believes, is one of the most powerful and enjoyable ways to introduce that culture to a wider audience, and he hopes to do so through his upcoming projects.
This Malaysia Day, Des hopes more people will recognise that, despite differences in culture, background and experience, everyone has a part to play in building a stronger society.
“The beauty of Malaysia is that we do not all have to be the same in order to stand together. Our diversity is our identity, and our unity is our strength.
“At the end of the day, despite our differences, we all share the same home.”

title: Pitching in: Leukemia survivor offers lifeline to young people coping with cancer
content:
The organizer: Geoff Eaton
The pitch: Founding Young Adult Cancer Canada
Geoff Eaton had barely graduated from Memorial University in St. John’s in 1998 when he was diagnosed with Leukemia. He was 22 years old and at one point doctors said he had less than a 2-per-cent chance of surviving.
After months of chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant from his father, Mr. Eaton’s health improved. At the time he was searching for an organization that offered support to young people coping with cancer. “We didn’t find anybody,” he recalled. “Young adult cancer is pretty new on the radar, and it wasn’t at all on the radar in the 2000s.”
That led Mr. Eaton to launch Young Adult Cancer Canada in 2000. The St. John’s-based charity provides a range of services to people between the ages of 15 and 39 who are living with cancer. YACC’s programs include chat groups, annual conferences, a four-day retreat and social connections. “We set out to be this national resource for these young adults,” said Mr. Eaton.
His own battle with cancer was far from over. In 2001 his Leukemia returned and he had another bone marrow transplant from his father. The transplant and treatments were a success and Mr. Eaton, now 50, is enjoying a full life with his wife and three children.
“There’s no question in my mind that I’m the luckiest person you’ve ever talked to in your life,” he said. “I’ve got a collection of miracles stacked up in my life, and I am very mindful of that.”
He’s continued to lead YACC as executive director and the charity supports nearly 8,000 young people across Canada. “Everything we do is centred on this notion of community,” he said.
YACC relies on donations, grants and sponsorships for its funding. This summer it received a major boost from the charitable arm of Spencer’s Gifts, a U.S.-based retailer with 50 outlets in Canada. Each of the Canadian stores is raising money for YACC from Aug. 20 to Sept. 13. “It’s a huge partnership for us,” said Mr. Eaton.
Mr. Eaton said his struggles with cancer have taught him that “there are good things in all of life’s challenges.”
“I really believe every win in our life is a team win, and that means at work and at home,” he added. “And YACC is a beautiful example of a team win.”

title: Edward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community space
content:
Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged.
The dean of Bristol, the Very Rev Mandy Ford, said Colston’s remains would probably stay where they were in All Saints church on one of Bristol’s busiest streets.
Colston, who died in 1721, made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue in the city centre was toppled during a Black Lives Matter protest and thrown into the harbour.
The diocese of Bristol has been consulting with Bristolians over what to do with All Saints on Corn Street, which has been closed since 1984.
While no final decision has yet been made, it seems likely it will be used as a space to reflect on the port’s connections with the slave trade – and Colston’s remains will stay where they are.
Ford said: “There is very, very clear guidance which assumes that you don’t disturb remains that have been given Christian burial, except in exceptional circumstances and so the presumption is that they will stay where they are.”
The dean said that if there was to be a radical rebuilding of the space there could be an argument to inter the remains elsewhere. “Otherwise the assumption is that Christian burial is permanent and that’s where they stay.”
Ford brings deep expertise to the job of helping decide what happens to Colston’s bones, as when she worked in Leicester she was closely involved in the reinterment of Richard III’s remains after they were found in a car park there.
She acknowledged people had different understandings of the theological or spiritual significance of human remains. “But it’s a Christian place of burial and we are a Christian church trying to do the right thing. This is the burial place of a human being who was involved in a practice which we recognise to be utterly sinful and wrong.”
The question of what to do about sites connected to Colston in Bristol is a thorny one.
After the Colston statue was thrown into the harbour, windows celebrating him were removed from two Bristol churches as the diocese declared the fall of the statue was a “signal” for it to take action. In the same year, Bristol’s concert hall was renamed Bristol Beacon, having previously been called Colston Hall.
It is likely to be many months before a final decision is made over the fate of All Saints.
But the dean said: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation. From the work that we’ve been doing in the cathedral and the relationships and the conversations that we have, I think there’s a strong sense that there’s huge potential in Bristol to have difficult conversations and to build a better future on the basis of truth-telling about the past.”
She added that work carried out at a new All Saints had the potential to sit alongside projects on Bristol’s history being done by institutions including the University of Bristol and Bristol Old Vic.
Ford said: “I think one can see it as part of a much bigger picture, which I think is really important if Bristol’s going to have a peaceful and flourishing future as a civic space and as a city.”
The Rev Anjali Kanagaratnam, who is leading the All Saints consultation, has been taking groups into the church.
She said there had been a huge range of views. “Each extreme was covered from: ‘I never want to come back into this building’ to ‘Why haven’t I been told that this building is here? I need to bring my children.’ Some people find it a hard space to be in. Some were annoyed by the fact that they didn’t know it was there.”
Kanagaratnam said it had been vital to hear the voices of people in Bristol that had been affected by transatlantic slavery but the church had also made sure it heard what people from other communities, such as white working-class areas in south Bristol.
Kanagaratnam said there was great potential for All Saints to be a place of “truth-telling”. She added: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation.”

title: Families, supporters mark 15th year of Indigenous woman’s disappearance
content:
Miles Morrisseau
ICT
In Winnipeg, Manitoba on Sept. 12, dozens of Indigenous peoples and supporters walked in memory of the late Tanya Nepinak who has been missing since 2011.
The walk started at the corner of Ellice Avenue and Sherbrook Street, where the then 31-year-old Nepinak of Pine Creek First Nations was last seen. The group marched past the Canadian Museum of Human Rights before ending up at the Odena Circle where prayers and songs were offered up in her memory.
Sue Caribou is Nepinak’s auntie and she thanked those in attendance for their support.
“I’m grateful and I’m very blessed there are so many beautiful people that remember our loved one and that she’s not forgotten or will not be forgotten,” Caribou told the crowd. “She doesn’t belong where she’s laying. We need justice, we need answers and we need to bring her home and rest beside her loved ones, not in a pile of trash.”
Nepinak was one case of many missing and murdered Indigenous women, some who were victims of serial killers targeting Indigenous women.
According to the Thomson Reuters 2025 report, “Missing and Stolen: Disappearances and Trafficking of Indigenous Peoples in Canada,” Manitoba accounts for 21 percent of all MMIW cases nationally from 2010 to April 2024. Winnipeg alone accounts for 14 percent of those disappearances.
Remains of Indigenous women have been found in two landfills sites, the Brady and Prairie Green Landfills.
Nepinak is believed to be in the Brady Landfill in Winnipeg.
Shawn Lamb, who targeted Indigenous women in the mid-2010s, was charged with the murder of Nepinak but the charges were stayed, or paused, leaving the case unresolved due to lack of evidence.
Lamb only served 13 years for manslaughter convictions in the deaths of 18-year-old Lorna Blacksmith from Pimicikamak Cree Nation and 25-year-old Carolyn Sinclair from Mathias Colomb Cree Nation, both who were wrapped in plastic and dumped in a Winnipeg back alley. Lamb was released in November 2025.
Lamb is one of two serial killers along with Jeremy Skibicki who targeted Indigenous women in Winnipeg.
Melissa Robinson is the head of the Missing and Murdered Peoples unit at the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs.
“For 15 years this family has been fighting and yelling and advocating to bring Tanya home. Fifteen years ago this should have happened. Here we are still standing here 15 years later waiting for them to go search that landfill to bring her home,” Robinson said. “My family fought to bring my cousin home and we did it in a very short time you know and why are we still waiting and wondering when it’s going to happen for Tanya.”
Robinson’s cousin, Morgan Harris, was one of the victims of serial killer, Jeremy Skibiki, who targeted Indigenous women and dumped their bodies in a Winnipeg landfill.
Family members and supporters set up a camp at the Brady Landfill to pressure the government to begin a search.
The provincial Conservative government at the time refused to begin the search stating that it would be expensive and dangerous and used the issue as a campaign platform to represent their fiscal responsibility.
They lost the election in October, 2023 and the New Democrat Party led by Wab Kinew, Anishinaabe, won a majority government and soon after announced that a search of the Prairie Green Landfill would commence.
The search discovered the remains of Harris and Marcedes Myran who were victims of Skibicki.
At the beginning of 2026 the search of the Brady Landfill began with the focus on Ashlee Shingoose who was given the spirit name Mashkode Bizhiki’ikwe, meaning Buffalo Woman, before her identity was revealed through DNA testing.
An official search for Nepinak has not begun.
“We wonder where she is or who took her. How come they’re not investigating? They’re not doing anything. They just want to forget about her,” Caribou told the gathering. “But I’m not gonna allow that. We need to work together. That’s the only way that it’s gonna happen, no more missing and murder, if we work together as one.”
Robinson told the crowd that they should be angered by the delay to search for Nepinak.
“I’m looking over at her daughter over there, Jasmine,” said Robinson. “When she was 10 years old lost her mother and knows where her mother lays. We should all be angry, we should all be upset and we should all be demanding that it happens now. No more waiting. I’m sick and tired of waiting. Tanya needs to come home, end of story.”

title: Bashir Hajiyev highlights revival of Kalbajar at Honey Festival
content:
Bashir Hajiyev highlights revival of Kalbajar at Honey Festival
- 12 September, 2026
- 19:18
It is a source of pride to gather again on this land and take part in an event that preserves Kalbajar's ancient traditions, Bashir Hajiyev, Special Representative of the President of Azerbaijan in Kalbajar district, said.
According to Report's correspondent in Karabakh, he made the remarks at the Second Kalbajar Honey Festival.
"We owe the fact that we are in our native land today to the decisive political will and leadership of the Victorious Commander-in-Chief, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, the heroism of our martyrs and the bravery of our veterans," Hajiyev said.
He noted that, on the instructions of the head of state, large-scale reconstruction and development work is underway in the liberated territories, settlements are being rebuilt and residents are gradually returning to their native lands.
"Kalbajar is one of the important centers of this large-scale reconstruction process. Life is becoming more vibrant here with each passing day, people are once again working on their native lands and establishing farms, while various events and festivals are being held. All this is a manifestation of the new reality created by the Great Return. The fact that the Honey Festival is being held in Kalbajar for the second time also carries special significance in this regard," he said.
Hajiyev noted that beekeeping is one of Kalbajar's traditional agricultural activities and has long played an important role in employment and the economic life of the district's residents.
"These traditions continue to develop today and are entering a new stage. It is particularly encouraging that beekeepers are expanding their activities and presenting their products at a festival like this," he said.
According to Hajiyev, events such as the Honey Festival are rooted in the hard work of Kalbajar residents, their love for their homeland and attachment to their native land.
"We clearly see these values today in their daily lives and in their enthusiastic participation in this event. Their work and attachment to the land give these events their true meaning. The joy on people's faces shows that such events are an expression of reunion with their land and the new life being built here," he said.
Hajiyev expressed confidence that the Honey Festival would continue to be held as a tradition, expand in scale from year to year and contribute to promoting Kalbajar's agricultural, tourism and economic potential both in Azerbaijan and internationally.
"I would like to thank everyone who contributed to organizing this festival, first and foremost the head of state, as well as our residents, beekeepers, farmers, guests and media representatives," he added.

title: Lethbridge firefighters honoured at annual memorial: ‘What we signed up to do’
content:
It’s been 25 years since terrorists attacked the United States by crashing two commercial passenger jets into the World Trade Centres, one into the Pentagon and another that was taken down by passengers over a field in Pennsylvania.
Thousands of people died that day. Many who lived through witnessing it remember the tragedy as if it was yesterday.
“I was still in high school. I was in math class, so I remember exactly where I was,” said Brent Nunweiler.
A few short years later, Nunweiler himself would become a firefighter, saying he was influenced by those in service to change his career plans.
Now, he is the president of the Local IAFF 237 Firefighters Union in Lethbridge.
Far removed from the attacks in the northeastern US, Lethbridge’s brothers and sisters in the red trucks still honour the fallen every year.
“Twenty-five years ago, our profession changed forever,” Nunweiler said. “We’re honoured to recognize those from, not only New York, but our own members here who have given their lives for the community.”
During the annual event, every IAFF member across North America who passed away in the last year is honoured by having their name called.
Get daily National news
In Lethbridge, all local members are read aloud, whether they passed away this past year, or decades ago.
“A lot of those names we read locally I worked with, (my colleagues) worked with. Their families are here, so to let their families know we are still thinking about them and that their service is honoured is extremely important,” said Nunweiler.
Most of the names of people called died, not actively battling a blaze, but to cancer.
It’s a silent killer that has claimed so many firefighters in the years since 9/11, and for generations before the attacks.
“Our risks stay with us long after we stay home. It’s a dangerous profession, one of the most dangerous in the world.
“None of us would choose a different profession, this is what we signed up to do.”
As this year marks a quarter-century since the attacks, it felt different for those involved in the ceremony.
“We always feel it every year, but this year we knew it was in the public awareness and lots of people have that history in their hearts,” said Neil Laboske, commander of the IAFF 237 honour guard.
He says sadness and grief is felt fully, but it’s not the only emotion relit every year on September 11.
“Immediately after the events of 9/11, everybody was very much together and working together on building a future,” he said.
That unity in the face of rubble and smoke defined the days, weeks and years after the attack.
Now, Laboske says it’s more important than ever to remain unified while honouring the fallen.
“We just hope it’s an opportunity for people to stop, look around and remember what’s really important.”

title: These girls fear new child protection laws will lead to 'lost generations'
content:
Tiwi Island teenagers reflect on changes to NT child protection laws
Surrounded by the ocean, where eucalypt forest stretches from the sand to meet the sky, the Tiwi Islands are a living library for the young people who call it home.
Etched into the landscape are guides on how to live off the land and language that describes their way of life, all of which has taught kids their traditional customs over generations.
The island and its community hold the knowledge that tells the story of each family and how they're connected.
But there are fears these connections to kin and culture are under threat.
These fears are acutely felt by 17-year-old Tiwi Island girls Shanina Kantilla and Tahni Thompson, who are cousins on their mother's side.
Even when they're hundreds of kilometres from home, the islands are never far from their minds.
Shanina recalls a happy childhood spent camping, hunting, swimming and fishing.
"It's very important, especially starting from a young age, learning about our culture, skin groups and also our country … where we inherit our tribes, the sacred sites, ceremony," she said.
Tahni also feels a deep connection to being Tiwi, having returned after spending part of her childhood in Darwin.
"It's like my safe place. Whenever I go to other places, I always feel homesick," she said.
Life on the Tiwi Islands
The Tiwi Islands is known for many things — vibrant artwork, secluded fishing spots and die-hard footy fans — with some of Australia's most renowned AFL players coming out of the region.
"We have a local league of AFL and it gets really hectic around those times," Tahni said.
Tiwi culture is also embedded in the girls' schooling, with weekly lessons on country.
But the real tutoring starts young and comes from within families — grandparents, parents, aunties and uncles.
Shanina's pride in her family traditions shines through as she explains how she's been taught to take wood from the local paper bark trees to weave into baskets.
"We scrape all the wood out and when we're done, we have to boil it and then we fold it, and let it sit for about two, three hours," she said.
"Once it dries up, we come back and start doing our traditional paintings."
Both girls are well aware past government policies prevented this cultural knowledge from being passed down.
"Since the missionaries came, they just changed everything," Tahni said.
"Some of the kids on the other island, [due to] the [Stolen] Generations, don't really speak Tiwi."
From the early 1900s, Catholic missions on the Tiwi Islands controlled much of daily life, influencing where people lived, who they married and the upbringing of their children.
For many families, the policies disrupted the transmission of language, cultural practices and traditional knowledge.
Today, cultural disconnection can take different forms.
Tahni knows this firsthand. Growing up away from her homelands, she felt as though a part of her identity was missing until she returned to the Tiwi Islands.
"I wouldn't want to be taken away from my family," she said.
"I would want to stay with them forever."
Deflating the 'political football'
On the other side of the territory's coastline, as thousands gathered for the Garma festival, First Nations people voiced fears of a renewed threat to kinship systems and culture.
Just weeks before, the Northern Territory government announced changes to child protection laws which critics said weakened the Aboriginal Child Placement Principle.
National Indigenous children's commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter was among those fearing it would lead to more children removed from their communities.
"I'm not here in a battle, I'm here to protect our children and make sure they're safe," she said.
"I feel like it's a bit of political football for everybody, and that's not what our kids should be."
The child placement principle aims to keep Aboriginal children connected to family, community and culture when they enter care.
It prioritises placing children with family in the first instance, then the child's own First Nations community and then other First Nations carers.
But under the NT changes, introduced after the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the government no longer needs to try to place a child with their community or a First Nations carer if they can't be placed with family.
Sue-Anne Hunter sees devastating echoes of the past.
"No-one is saying that our children need to be unsafe. If a child needs to be removed, then that's the fact. The thing is that culture is part of safety. It's their identity," she said.
"Maybe they [the NT government] need to have a discussion with some Stolen Generation people about how being disconnected affected their lives."
Ms Hunter spent much of her time at Garma hearing directly from young people, many of whom told her they were anxious about the changes.
"It's front of mind for youth as well," she said.
"We need to be investing in the front end. Family support, getting into families early, not waiting until we're ready to remove them."
A spokesperson for the NT government denied the changes were weakening protections for Aboriginal children.
"These reforms — designed after extensive consultation — created a Universal Child Placement Principle so the same strong provisions apply to every child," they said.
"Additional provisions have been retained for Aboriginal children that reflect their cultural needs and connection to family, community and country."
Child protection isn't the only policy change adding to Ms Hunter's workload.
In recent years the NT lowered the age of criminal responsibility and reintroduced spit hoods, the NT, Victoria and Queensland removed the principle of detention as a last resort for children, Victoria and Queensland brought in "adult crime, adult time" laws and nearly all jurisdictions tightened youth bail.
Ms Hunter said she wished the politicians who attended Garma, including NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, had asked the next generation what they thought of the changes.
"There are a whole lot of people here ready to give some solutions, have some discussions, but it just doesn't seem to be happening," she said.
"It would have been nice if [Ms Finocchiaro] was able to stay, maybe go into the youth forum and listen to the kids."
The NT government spokesperson said lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 10 was about "early intervention and community safety".
"Strong families, cultural connection and early intervention are the best way to break the cycle of youth crime, alongside clear consequences when offending occurs," they said.
'They are just little kids'
Inside the youth forum, Tahni and Shanina reflected on family and friends who had been caught up in the justice system or removed from their families.
"Those ones that are under Territory Families [in out-of-home-care], they don't know our culture much because they only come once a year for a visit around the community," Shanina said.
"It's hard for them to know who their family is, who they are, and their culture … I feel for them."
They were also worried about children as young as 10 being held responsible for crimes.
"Ten years old, they're not really teenagers yet, they are just little kids. They aren't mature enough [to understand]," Tahni said.
"Instead of sending them away, just discipline them on the island and that way they can learn from their mistakes instead of getting them sent off somewhere else.
"[Juvenile detention is] pretty traumatic, and they'll have to carry that trauma for the rest of their lives."
The cousins say there are deeper issues affecting young people and punishment isn't the solution.
"I think younger children have to do counselling, talk about their feelings … instead of getting frustrated. That causes a lot of problems," Shanina said.
As the youth forum began to wind up, Tahni shared her message for the NT government.
"Our voice matters," she said.
"We don't want [Stolen Generations] to happen again.
"If we didn't have culture, we wouldn't know our identity. That's why it's important for us to learn at a young age.
"[Otherwise] there might not be any Tiwi people left. There will just be lost generations."

title: Lambayeque: el distrito de Incahuasi celebrará los 50 años del festival folclórico Takin
content:
El distrito de Incahuasi, en la provincia lambayecana de Ferreñafe, se prepara para celebrar por todo lo alto las bodas de oro del Festival Folclórico Incahuasi Takin, una edición histórica que, por primera vez, tendrá carácter internacional y reunirá expresiones ancestrales de Perú y otros países de la región norteña.


En diálogo con la agencia Andina, el presidente del comité organizador del festival, Armando Sánchez Céspedes, anunció que la celebración congregará a danzantes y músicos de Ecuador y Colombia, además de delegaciones de Cajamarca, Amazonas y Ayacucho, y representantes de las comunidades de Cañaris, Penachí, La Ramada y otros pueblos de la zona andina de Lambayeque.
El encuentro se desarrollará en el distrito andino de Incahuasi del 19 al 23 de setiembre y busca convertirse en una gran plataforma para preservar y difundir la cultura quechua.
La programación incluye la elección de la hipash (señorita en quechua) del festival, presentaciones musicales, participación de unos 200 niños de 2 a 5 años, así como estudiantes de primaria y secundaria que mostrarán danzas, costumbres y otros códigos culturales.
Las comunidades y sus sabios
Uno de los momentos centrales será la participación de las comunidades y sus sabios con cerca de 300 comuneros que exhibirán diversas manifestaciones culturales. También se rendirá homenaje a los hombres y las mujeres que contribuyeron durante décadas a mantener vigente esta tradición ancestral.
La Municipalidad Distrital de Incahuasi ha destinado alrededor de 48,000 soles en premios, que serán distribuidos entre cerca de 70 expresiones culturales, entre ellas, cantantes que interpretarán temas en quechua y agrupaciones de danzantes.
El también gestor cultural indígena y profesor quechua Armando Sánchez destacó que esta edición representa una verdadera celebración de la resistencia cultural. Recordó que el Takin atravesó una etapa crítica y estuvo cerca de desaparecer, pero el trabajo sostenido de las comunidades permitió recuperar su vigencia.
Rescatar lo más auténtico
“Queremos rescatar lo más originario, lo más auténtico”, remarcó Sánchez, al advertir que algunas expresiones tradicionales han sufrido procesos de estilización con el paso del tiempo. Por ello, el festival busca recuperar las vestimentas, danzas, música y costumbres en su forma ancestral.
Refirió que la expectativa también es turística. Luego de recibir unos 7,500 visitantes el año pasado, los organizadores proyectan superar las 10,000 personas en esta edición, entre turistas, visitantes nacionales, residentes que retornan a su tierra y ciudadanos extranjeros.
El alcalde de Incahuasi, Jesús Vilcabana Manayay, resaltó que el festival representa una oportunidad para mostrar al Perú y al mundo la riqueza cultural del distrito, donde se mantienen vigentes el idioma quechua, la vestimenta tradicional, la artesanía, la gastronomía y los saberes transmitidos por generaciones.
Cultura ancestral
Por su parte, el director del museo Nacional Sicán, arqueólogo Carlos Elera Arévalo, expresó que a cinco décadas de su creación, el Takin busca demostrar que la cultura ancestral no pertenece únicamente al pasado. Está viva en sus niños, sus comunidades, sus músicos, sus danzantes y sus sabios, y ahora se proyecta desde las alturas de Lambayeque hacia el escenario internacional.
Desde el ámbito cultural, representantes de la Dirección Desconcentrada de Cultura respaldaron la celebración y destacaron que Incahuasi constituye una expresión viva del patrimonio andino de Lambayeque.

title: Pacific chiefs to attend Māori Queen's second koroneihana
content:
Pacific chiefs to attend Māori Queen's second koroneihana
The bond between the Pacific and the whare ariki o Te Wherowhero (the house of chief Te Wherowhero) continues to grow stronger ahead of reigning Māori Queen Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po's second koroneihana (coronation) celebrations, a Kiingitanga spokesperson says.
Pacific traditional leaders to gather at Maori koroneihana
Ariki (chiefs) from across the Pacific will congregate onto Tūrangawaewae Marae (the official headquarters of the Kiingitanga)later this week, embodying an age-old connection, through whakapapa (genealogy), reo (language) and culture.
Kiingitanga spokesperson Rahui Papa said the ancient connections between the Kiingitanga movement (Māori King movement) and the great houses of the Pacific was solidified nearly 100 years ago.
"In the 1940's, Princess Te Puea went with the then Princess Piki, who later became Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu, [and] they travelled extensively across the Pacific," Papa said.
"They met with Queen Sālote and attended the double weddings of her sons. They met with Pa Ariki in the Cook Islands, in Aitutaki, [meeting chiefs] in Samoa, in Tonga, and in various places across the Pacific."
Papa said Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu played a role in establishing the South Pacific Forum, now know as the Pacific Islands Forum, which was having its annual leaders meeting in Palau this week.
"In the times of Te Arikinui Te Atairangikaahu, they set up the South Pacific Forum with big names, like Malietoa (Tanumafili II) of Samoa, Ratu [Sir Kamisese] Mara of Fiji, the King of Tonga Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV. A whole lot of those connections are still happening today."
Papa shared a fond memory from Te Atairangikaahu's silver anniversary in 1991, the familial connection between all the chiefs from across Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia who attended the celebration.
"I think it was Uncle Koro Wētere [who] talked about the Pacific Ocean as it laps the shores of all of our cousins countries as well as Aotearoa as the connector. Those waves, that ocean was the connector of us, not just in a physical sense, but in a cultural and spiritual sense as well."
He said Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po has visited and hosted these ariki at various Kiingitanga events during her two years as arikinui, continuing the legacy her tupuna (ancestors).
"Like Queen Sālote and King Tōfa'ahau. With Ratu Mara, for example, and [Ro] Lady Lala [Mara] who have passed, now their son has taken a leadership role within the [Great] Council of Chiefs in Fiji," Papa said.
As the new generation of ariki continue to stoke these fires of connection, Papa believed it could be an example the world could take note of.
"With the wars that are happening around Europe and in other places, the Pacific holds a very, very special key to world nationhood, to world whanaungatanga (relationships).
"I think that there are beautiful examples that we can share with the world in the hopes of bringing everyone into the cultural dynamic that is just part of our DNA."
The ariki are scheduled to be welcomed on Friday morning with Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro leading the group onto the atea.

title: Toolkit helping sports clubs create a place for all
content:
Comment: Sport can be one of the most powerful places in a young person’s life. It’s where friendships and friendly rivalries are formed, confidence grows, and resilience develops. It’s where many of us learn teamwork, leadership and what it feels like to belong. It’s where we find joy.
Every young, and not so young, person deserves the opportunity to experience that.
Yet, for many takatāpui, transgender, non-binary and MVPFAFF+ people in Aotearoa, sport is a place where they are left wondering whether they will be welcomed at all.
Every season missed is a lost opportunity for connection, belonging and wellbeing.
Every young person who walks away from sport because adults don’t know how to respond is a loss for that young person, their team, their community, and sport as a whole.
That is the reality for many. Research from the Counting Ourselves survey found 45 percent of transgender people in Aotearoa have avoided sports teams or clubs because they did not feel welcome. Only 14 percent of transgender and non-binary people had participated in organised physical activity in the previous four weeks, compared with 26 percent of the general population.
The responsibility should never sit with a person to change who they are to participate, but with the organisations, clubs and teams to create environments where people know they belong. Too often we ask a person to justify themselves, to prove something, to fit in. But we all know a sense of belonging comes from being able to show up as yourself and be welcomed as you are.
And for those of us who are kaitiaki of the sports system, as clubs, codes, coaches, volunteers, leaders and supporters, we have a clear opportunity to do better.
That’s the kaupapa behind the Transgender Inclusion in Community Sport Toolkit, developed by WISPA and InsideOUT Kōaro, with support from the Clare Foundation.
The toolkit is a free, practical resource co-designed across both organisations, grounded in research, lived experience, and case studies from our own sport sector. Rather than prescribing one approach for every sport, it helps organisations ask better questions and make informed decisions.
The toolkit invites organisations to start with four key questions:
- What parameters of unfairness does your sport already tolerate?
- Does the evidence actually show transgender participants exceeding those parameters?
- Is the issue in a given situation really about someone being transgender, or is it skill, technique, height, weight, or bias?
- And on what grounds is safety being assessed?
These questions matter because sport already accommodates enormous differences between participants.
Take football for example. Junior teams are grouped by age, and young people develop at wildly different rates – one team can have huge gaps in height, strength, and technical ability. In senior football, nothing stops a Football Fern turning up to play a community game on a Sunday.
You learn fast which opposition players have a ‘big boot’, and to duck when they line one up. We may complain about it, but talent, training and physical variations are part of every game we play.
History also reminds us that exclusion is rarely justified in hindsight.
Women were banned from many sports, such as football, rugby, cycling and marathon running for much of the last century, often using arguments about fairness, safety, “protecting” women, and the integrity of sport. Many of those bans only lifted after the 1970s. We’re still paying for it, still pursuing equity in resources, support, and attitudes towards female athletes.
We’re watching the same instinct play out again now, aimed at transgender people. Too often conversations about transgender inclusion start with reasons why inclusion might be difficult rather than asking how we make it possible.
The toolkit seeks to shift that conversation by providing organisations with a practical headstart. It’s built around five pou: inclusion; wellbeing and safety; privacy and dignity; listening and responding; and learning and knowledge.
It provides actions, policy guidance, case studies, and resources that clubs can put into practice immediately. The toolkit also includes a policy template and an inclusive language guide so organisations don’t have to start from a blank page.
The numbers show the opportunity in front of us: to make community sport a place where takatāpui, transgender, and non-binary people know they are expected, welcomed and supported. The participation gap is easily addressed by taking a practical, values-led approach to community building. This is ongoing, relational work.
Next time fairness is raised about anyone, we encourage people to start with the four questions, challenge assumptions, and stay curious. Aotearoa has always been strongest when it chooses inclusion over exclusion and, in doing so, preserves the wellbeing, dignity, and joy of its rangatahi.

유엔 아동권리 보고서로 소년병 참상 고발
조혼·여성할례 철폐 등 여성·아동 인권 헌신
구글 검색에서 연합뉴스 기사를 우선적으로 보여줍니다.
(서울=연합뉴스) 성도현 기자 = 한 나라의 퍼스트레이디가 된다는 것은 결코 쉬운 일이 아니다. 그러나 '넬슨 만델라의 미망인'으로 통하는 그라사 마셸은 역사상 유일하게 두 나라의 영부인을 지냈다.
모잠비크의 독립운동가였던 마셸은 남편이었던 사모라 마셸 모잠비크 대통령이 세상을 떠난 뒤 남아프리카공화국의 민주화 영웅 넬슨 만델라 대통령과 결혼해 두 나라의 퍼스트레이디가 됐다.
하지만 마셸을 단순히 영부인으로만 기억한다면 그의 삶을 제대로 설명할 수 없다. 그는 교사이자 독립운동가, 정치인으로 출발해 평생 여성과 아동의 인권을 위해 목소리를 낸 국제 인권운동가다.
마셸은 1945년 당시 포르투갈 식민지였던 모잠비크에서 태어났다.
이후 수도 마푸투의 명문 고등학교를 거쳐 포르투갈 리스본대학교에서 유학하며 독문학을 전공했다. 유학 시절 다양한 배경의 학생들과 교류하며 식민 체제에 문제의식을 가졌다.
특히 유학 시절 모잠비크의 독립을 이끌던 민족해방전선(FRELIMO)에 참여하면서 조국의 자유를 되찾겠다는 신념으로 유학을 포기하고 귀국했다.
이후 1973년 탄자니아로 건너가 민족해방전선의 게릴라 훈련을 받고, 독립운동에 적극적으로 뛰어들었다.
1975년 모잠비크가 포르투갈로부터 독립하자, 사모라 마셸 초대 대통령은 그를 교육문화부 장관으로 임명했다.
마셸은 1989년까지 장관으로 재직하며 식민 통치로 인해 90%가 넘었던 모잠비크의 문해율을 낮추고자 노력했다. 학교를 대거 설립하면서 더 많은 어린이와 젊은이들이 학교에 갈 수 있도록 교육 체계를 세우는 일에 힘을 쏟았다.
이 시기에 그는 사모라 마셸 대통령과 동지에서 연인으로 발전해 결혼했다.
모잠비크의 발전을 이끌며 승승장구했지만, 갑자기 시련이 닥쳤다. 1986년 남편 마셸 대통령이 탄 전용기가 남아공 국경 인근에서 추락하면서 남편을 잃었고, 영부인 자리에서도 물러났다.
하지만 그는 슬픔에만 빠지지 않았고, 전 세계에서 고통받는 아이들을 향해 눈을 돌렸다.
1990년 유엔(UN) 사무총장의 요청을 받아 무력 분쟁이 아동의 삶을 어떻게 파괴하는지에 관해 조사한 후 보고서를 제출했다. 이 작업은 국제사회의 분쟁지역 아동 보호 논의에 큰 영향을 미쳤다.
그가 작성한 유엔아동기금(유니세프) 보고서는 전 세계 분쟁 지역에서 소년병들이 총알받이로 동원되고, 아동들이 끔찍한 인권 유린에 노출되는 참상을 적나라하게 고발했다.
또 이후 유엔이 아동 보호를 위한 특별 대표를 신설하고, 관련 국제법을 강화하는 데 결정적인 역할을 했다.
1998년 마셸은 만델라의 80세 생일에 결혼식을 올리면서 다시 유명세를 치렀다. 모잠비크에 이어 이웃나라 남아공의 영부인이 됐다.
물론 마셸은 대통령의 배우자라는 역할에만 머물지 않았다. 만델라와 함께 국제사회의 평화와 인권 문제에 목소리를 냈고, 여성과 아동의 권리 증진을 위한 활동을 계속했다.
2007년에는 만델라와 함께 전 세계의 전직 지도자들이 모여 평화와 인권 문제를 해결하는 글로벌 평화 그룹인 '디 엘더스'의 창립 멤버가 됐다.
특히 그는 아프리카 사회의 오랜 악습인 '조혼'과 '여성 할례' 철폐 운동에 앞장섰다.
또 여성들이 빈곤과 차별의 피해자에 머물러서는 안 되며, 경제와 정치의 주체가 돼야 한다고 강조했다. 이 신념을 바탕으로 여성의 경제적 자립과 교육, 건강, 정치 참여를 확대하는 활동을 꾸준히 이어갔다.
2010년에는 '그라사 마셸 트러스트'를 설립해 아프리카 여성의 경제·금융 역량 강화, 교육, 식량안보와 영양, 좋은 거버넌스 등을 지원하고 있다.
이러한 그의 노력은 국제적으로도 인정받았다. 난민 아동을 비롯한 인도주의 활동으로 유엔 난센 난민상을 받았고, 2018년에는 여성·아동·청소년의 건강과 복지에 기여한 공로로 세계보건기구(WHO) 골드메달을 받았다.
현재도 여성과 아동의 권리를 옹호하는 국제적 활동가로서 좋은 거버넌스와 사회적 불평등 문제를 다루고 있다. 아프리카 곳곳에서 마셸 여사를 '대륙의 어머니'로 부르는 이유다.

title: La gerontolescencia
content:
La revolución de la longevidad ha comenzado en el mundo. La gerontolescencia significa -no un programa privado de envejecimiento activo y autónomo-, sino el descubrimiento de una nueva etapa de la vida de hombres y mujeres, entre los 65 y 80 años de edad, reconocida por la Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS).
Su creador es el investigador Alexandre Karachi, quien, junto a otros estudiosos del envejecimiento, como Pere Estupinyá en la obra “Qué quieres ser de mayor”, proporcionan las claves para afrontar el paso de los años con ilusión, mediante una base psicológica y social, física y médica.
La propuesta es clara: promover un envejecimiento activo para lograr una buena salud con autonomía. Según la OMS, la gerontolescencia corresponde a un nuevo período vital, entre la adultez y la vejez (65-80 años), que implica el ejercicio de un derecho humano a disfrutar de un envejecimiento activo y pleno, sentirse jóvenes de cuerpo y espíritu, y contribuir a la sociedad con experiencias y conocimientos.
La edad biológica es importante para los gerontolescentólogos, pero más aún la edad psicológica cuya impronta es la plenitud, entendida como el proceso vital que conjuga la totalidad del ser humano: encontrar sentido para vivir y seguir viviendo, en relación con otras personas, el movimiento, la alimentación sana y la naturaleza. Así, la plenitud vital se articula con la plenitud ocupacional.
Los gerontolescentes son abuelos y jubilados. Esta condición les permite aprovechar al máximo la esperanza de vida vigente y fortalecerla, mediante estrategias que combinen, de manera equilibrada, la salud física, mental y emocional.
La OMS ha reconocido que el mapa de la población mundial está cambiando, por el control de las enfermedades globales, y las políticas públicas en salud que aplican los gobiernos. En el Ecuador, la esperanza de vida al nacer (2024) se cifra en 77.58 años promedio. Las mujeres en 80.31 años, y los hombres en 74.88 años. El país ocupa el número 66, que corresponde a la parte media entre las naciones del orbe.
Las Naciones Unidas han comenzado a debatir este tema. El Estado ecuatoriano tiene una deuda con los adultos mayores, especialmente con aquellos que no están afiliados al seguro social. De ahí que es necesario que se diseñen políticas públicas para este sector de población, que sufre carencias y exclusiones. ¡El reconocimiento de la gerontolescencia es un gran paso!

title: Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld hielpen vorig jaar meer dan 5.000 slachtoffers, vooral vrouwen en meisjes
content:
De Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld (ZSG) in ons land hebben in het afgelopen jaar meer dan 5.000 slachtoffers opgevangen. Dat blijkt uit nieuwe cijfers van de centra. 9 op de 10 slachtoffers zijn meisjes en vrouwen. Vaak is de pleger een bekende, zoals een (ex)-partner, vriend of kennis.
Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld hielpen vorig jaar meer dan 5.000 slachtoffers, vooral vrouwen en meisjes
Heb je een vraag over seksueel geweld? Dan kan je terecht bij de hulplijn 1712. Voor een gesprek kan je ook 24/7 terecht bij Tele-Onthaal op het nummer 106. Je kan ook chatten via www.tele-onthaal.be . Jongeren kunnen terecht bij Awel op het telefoonnummer 102, via chat op awel.be , of bij chathulplijn Nupraatikerover.be .
Wil je medische, psychologische en/of juridische hulp, kan je terecht bij 1 van de (voorlopig) 10 Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld , ook via e-mail of telefoon.
Tussen de oprichting in 2017 en 2025 zijn al meer dan 22.500 slachtoffers opgevangen in een van de Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld in ons land. Daar kan je als slachtoffer van seksueel geweld gratis en de klok rond terecht voor medische, forensische en psychologische hulp. Je kan er ook sporen laten verzamelen en aangifte doen bij de politie.
In het grootste deel van de gevallen waren de slachtoffers meisjes en vrouwen (90 procent). Voor het merendeel van de slachtoffers (62 procent) is de pleger een bekende, zoals een huisgenoot, (ex-)partner, vriend of kennis. De gemiddelde leeftijd van de slachtoffers is 24 jaar.
Vorig jaar lag het aantal slachtoffers dat zich meldde op meer dan 5.000. Het aantal stijgt al enkele jaren, al is die stijging grotendeels te verklaren doordat het aantal centra en de bekendheid ervan toenemen. Niet omdat het fenomeen steeds toeneemt, klinkt het.
België telt in totaal 10 Zorgcentra na Seksueel Geweld. Dit jaar nog worden 3 bijkomende centra geopend: in het UZ Jette, in het ziekenhuis van Doornik en in Ottignies, in Waals-Brabant. Het Instituut voor de Gelijkheid van Vrouwen en Mannen (IGVM) coördineert en ondersteunt mee de zorgcentra.
Documentaire
De voorstelling van de cijfers in Cinema Palace in Brussel ging gepaard met de vertoning van een nieuwe documentaire, 'The sessions', genaamd. Die geeft een inkijk in het verwerkingsproces van een jonge vrouw die het slachtoffer werd van seksueel geweld.
Vanaf 30 september loopt de documentaire in bioscopen en culturele centra. Vanaf januari 2027 is de docu ook te zien op VRT Canvas en VRT MAX.

title: Lower fees, more places in facilities for PWDs among first moves by disability task force
content:
Lower fees, more places in facilities for PWDs among first moves by disability task force
- By 2028, the Singapore government will lower fees and increase subsidies for disability services, benefiting around 5,000 people with disabilities and making care more affordable for families.
- The government will add 1,300 more spaces to day activity centres and sheltered workshops by 2030, easing long waiting lists and helping PWDs build skills and community ties.
- Subsidy eligibility will expand to more middle-income households, with fee caps introduced and costs for families with higher support needs dropping by up to 80%, easing financial stress on caregivers.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – By 2028, families will pay less for disability services, as the Government lowers fees and increases means-tested subsidies.
More spaces will also be added to day activity centres and sheltered workshops by 2030.
Around 5,000 people with disabilities (PWDs) accessing community and residential disability services are expected to benefit from these changes by 2030.
Fee caps for all government-funded disability services will be introduced, with the amounts varying for different facilities.
For most families, subsidy rates will rise by at least 10 percentage points. These subsidies are means-tested, and apply to a wide range of disability services, including day activity centres, adult disability hostels and homes.
The income ceiling for households to qualify for these subsidies will also be raised. The maximum per capita monthly household income will increase from $4,800 to $6,000.
This will extend financial support to more middle-income households, and covers about 80 per cent of households with PWDs, said the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).
These moves to make disability services more affordable are among the first set of recommendations by the Taskforce on Assurance for Families with Persons with Disabilities released on Sept 17.
The task force was formed in December 2025 to review how support for the PWD community can be strengthened across life stages, and has held several engagement sessions with groups including families and service providers.
Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development Goh Pei Ming, who leads the task force with four other political office-holders, announced the moves on the sidelines of a visit to the TOUCH Centre for Independent Living at the Enabling Village in Lengkok Bahru.
Goh said affordability was one of the biggest concerns for caregivers, and some had expressed uncertainty about meeting their loved ones’ care needs over their lifetime.
“Over time, care costs can add up. Families hope to get assurances that support will continue to be affordable,” he said.
Another key move tackles a growing waiting list for day activity centres and sheltered workshops – facilities where adults with disabilities can be engaged in daily activities.
MSF will add another 1,300 day activity centre and sheltered workshop spaces by 2030, on top of the 1,000 additional places previously announced in 2024.
Goh said this “significant expansion” would bring the total number to about 5,800 places.
Families had told the task force that long wait times for such services can be stressful, he added.
Day activity centres are community-based facilities for those with disabilities who are aged 18 and above and cannot work, while sheltered workshops provide work skills training and job support for those with disabilities who can work, but are unable to or not yet ready to take up open employment.
Full recommendations to come in October
Costs for disability services were last adjusted in July 2026, when the Government increased subsidies for residential and community disability services by up to 15 per cent and 10 per cent respectively, and raised the household per capita income ceiling for subsidies from $3,600 to $4,800.
With the newest announcements, families of those with higher support needs will see their monthly fees after government subsidies for selected services drop by about 25 per cent to 80 per cent.
Lower-income households will pay no more than $10 per month for community-based services such as the day activity centres and Enabling Skills for Life Programme (ESLP), down from between $20 and $60 today.
The ESLP equips adult PWDs with independent living, communication, social-emotional functioning and vocational skills.
The Government will work with social service agencies over the next few years to expand capacity and carry out the adjustments to fees and subsidies, said MSF.
The inter-agency task force, which has looked into areas such as employment and lifelong learning for PWDs, will announce its full set of recommendations in early October.
Health product distributor Wu Ping’s son Sherman Jian, 24, has multiple disabilities and has attended the TOUCH Centre for Independent Living since 2021. Any additional savings will give the middle-income family more room to plan for his future, said the 56-year-old.
They currently pay $660 monthly for him to attend the day activity centre after government subsidies, down from $1,135 previously before the July adjustments.
Their out-of-pocket costs are likely to fall further with the latest changes.
She said in Mandarin: “These subsidies make me feel that it’s not only the family and parents caring for the child... There are people walking with us on this journey.”

title: Netball team's emotion-filled win after player killed in car crash
content:
Netball team's emotion-filled win after player killed in car crash
In short:
An A-grade netball team in Victoria's Wimmera region has won a high-emotion grand final after one of its most talented young players died in a car crash this week.
The Navarre Grasshoppers beat the Carisbrook Redbacks 58-51 in the Maryborough Castlemaine District Netball League decider.
What's next?
The team has been celebrated for its bravery, skill and determination, to win the game in honour of teammate Zanaiya Bergen.
The Navarre Grasshoppers have triumphed in a scenario no sporting team should ever have to face.
One of their most talented young players, 23-year-old Zanaiya Bergen, died on Thursday evening when her car hit a tree after training.
She and her teammates were on the verge of making history, after snapping Avoca's 69-game winning streak in a thrilling Maryborough Castlemaine District Netball League (MCDNL) preliminary final just days earlier.
In what was Zanaiya's debut season in the MCDNL, the goal shooter was one of five Navarre players named in the team of the year.
Her unexpected death cast doubt on whether her team would even play on Saturday.
Do it for Zee
Zanaiya, or Zee as she was affectionately known, had played 18 games for her new club, scoring 664 goals across the 2026 season.
She had previously featured in A-grade matches for Stawell in the Wimmera Football Netball League, and Rupanyup in the Horsham District Football Netball League.
MCDNL netball coordinator Katrina Turner said the league had spent most of Friday speaking with the Navarre Football Netball Club about whether the finals would go ahead.
"Whatever they decided, we would fully support them with what they wanted to do," Ms Turner said.
"When they called and said they wanted to play, I called their opponents in the A-grade and C-grade to let them know."
Zanaiya's name remained on the scoresheet for Saturday's grand final, and a minute's silence was held at the start of the game.
Purple ribbons and black arm bands were worn to mark the tragedy.
As the day went on, a significant crowd surrounded the Princes Park netball court at Maryborough to witness an A-grade match which was tense, competitive, and above all, highly emotive.
Zanaiya's teammates were doing all they could to win in honour of their teammate.
Emotion overcame some players as the game neared its end, and despite the heartbreaking circumstances, as the final whistle was blown the Navarre Grasshoppers came away with the win, 58-51.
Video of the match showed some players overwhelmed with tears the moment the game finished.
Members of the Navarre Football Netball Club have been offered counselling.
A premiership medal will go to Zanaiya's family.
Tributes far and wide
Zanaiya has been remembered as a funny, energetic, loyal and kind person.
Outside of her netball accolades, she spent five and a half years as a personal aged care worker at Eventide Homes in Stawell.
Her employer posted a social media tribute, which said Zanaiya brought warmth, laughter, kindness and genuine connection to every interaction.
"Zee leaves behind an enormous hole in our workplace and, most importantly, in the hearts of the residents and people she cared for so deeply," the post read.
"We will miss her more than words can express and will forever be grateful that she was part of our Eventide family."
